result.output:
# Lobu — Open-source backend for AI teammates

**Lobu** is open-source infrastructure for autonomous agents that **watch**, **remember**, and **act** where your team already works. Connect company tools, build living memory, and let agents run on schedules, in Slack threads, or over MCP — with sandboxed execution per user or channel and credentials agents never see.

Under the hood, workers run Lobu's Pi-based agent loop (bash, files, MCP tools, skills) inside an isolated sandbox per conversation. One Node process serves many agents and channels; shared memory and connectors live in Postgres (pgvector). Embed agents in your product, or give your team their own without running a separate instance per person.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d72a9286-0325-4b8b-afc0-c1efe9c96f4e

## Two ways in

### 1. Full agent — Slack, Telegram, behaviors, connectors

Scaffold and run locally with the CLI. Lobu boots as a single Node process with zero-config embedded Postgres by default (or bring your own — pgvector required — via `DATABASE_URL`). `lobu run` opens the web UI on `:8787` and can wire Slack via the hosted bot or your own app.

```bash
npx @lobu/cli@latest init my-bot
cd my-bot
npx @lobu/cli@latest run                      # boots the stack and applies your agent
npx @lobu/cli@latest chat -c local "hello"    # talk to it
```

`lobu run` auto-applies your `lobu.config.ts`, so the scaffolded agent is usable immediately. To use an external Postgres, set `DATABASE_URL` in `.env`; to push later config changes, run `lobu apply`.

Next steps: [Getting started](https://lobu.ai/getting-started/) (project layout, develop with your coding agent, evals) · [Memory](https://lobu.ai/getting-started/memory/) · [Skills](https://lobu.ai/getting-started/skills/) · [Channels](#channels)

### 2. Memory for Claude Code (and Claude Desktop)

Give Claude durable, structured memory via MCP — the same graph your Lobu agents use. Full setup: [Connect from Claude](https://lobu.ai/connect-from/claude/).

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http lobu https://lobu.ai/mcp   # or http://localhost:8787/mcp locally
```

Complete the OAuth flow when prompted, then enable the connector. Pair it with a project instruction or skill that tells Claude when to search memory and when to save what it learned.

Works the same for [ChatGPT](https://lobu.ai/connect-from/chatgpt/) and other MCP clients — one memory backend across clients.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Slack[Slack] <--> GW[Gateway]
  Telegram[Telegram] <--> GW
  WhatsApp[WhatsApp] <--> GW
  Discord[Discord] <--> GW
  API[REST API] <--> GW
  MCP[MCP clients] <--> GW

  GW <--> PG[(Postgres)]
  GW -->|spawn| W[Worker]

  subgraph Sandbox
    W
  end

  W -.->|HTTP proxy| GW
  W -.->|MCP proxy| GW
  GW -->|domain filter| Internet((Internet))
  GW -->|scoped tokens| ExtMCP[MCP Servers]
```

## Capabilities

Most agent stacks treat MCP as the memory: every turn, the agent calls GitHub, Slack, and CRM tools to reconstruct what happened. That knowledge stays siloed in the session and disappears when the chat ends.

Lobu runs a **data pipeline** instead. Connectors poll and webhooks push into one durable, append-only event log. Behaviors and chat agents read the same org-scoped knowledge graph — typed entities, relationships, searchable events — so anyone can resume where the organization left off, not where one conversation left off.

### Memory — ingest, entities, behaviors

**Ingest.** [Connectors](https://lobu.ai/sdks/connectors/) pull on a schedule; webhooks and the [REST API](https://lobu.ai/sdks/rest-api/) push. Stripe charges, GitHub PRs, form submissions, and connector polls all land as rows in the same log — a stable record of what happened in the world, not something the agent has to re-fetch through MCP every turn.

**Entities.** You define the schema (`Company`, `Project`, `Incident`, …) in `lobu.config.ts`. Events attach to entity instances (`Company:Acme`) and build a live knowledge graph the whole org shares. Corrections supersede old facts; nothing is deleted, so provenance and time-travel stay intact.

**Behaviors.** Standing goals on a cron or tight interval: read new rows in the log (including webhook-fed events like `pull_request.opened`), extract structured memory onto dynamic entities, and optionally run a [reaction](https://lobu.ai/sdks/reactions/) to notify Slack, open a ticket, or kick off agent work — while nobody is in chat.

Docs: [Memory](https://lobu.ai/getting-started/memory/) · [Connectors](https://lobu.ai/sdks/connectors/) · [Reactions](https://lobu.ai/sdks/reactions/)

### Agents — read the graph, branch to act

Chat agents **look up** what the pipeline already captured — search entities, read the event log, pull thread history — then **branch** into an isolated sandbox ([just-bash](https://www.npmjs.com/package/just-bash) + Nix) to run bash, edit files, and call MCP tools for side effects. MCP is for *doing*; the knowledge graph is for *knowing*. Pick any of [16 LLM providers](https://lobu.ai/reference/providers/); credentials stay on the gateway.

Behavior comes from a **role file model** — `IDENTITY.md` (who), `SOUL.md` (rules), `USER.md` (context). **Guardrails** gate input, output, and tool calls (`secret-scan`, `pii-scan`, inline LLM judges) so policy holds even when the prompt doesn't. Destructive MCP calls wait for in-thread approval; every action writes back to the log.

Docs: [Agent workspace](https://lobu.ai/guides/agent-prompts/) · [Guardrails](https://lobu.ai/guides/guardrails/) · [Security](https://lobu.ai/guides/security/)

### Channels

One instance serves **Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Teams, Google Chat**, and a [REST API](https://lobu.ai/reference/api-reference/) [![API Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/API_Docs-0096FF?style=for-the-badge&logo=readme&logoColor=white)](https://lobu.ai/reference/api-reference/). Each channel/DM gets its own runtime, model, tools, credentials, and Nix packages. Platform setup: [Slack](https://lobu.ai/platforms/slack/) · [Telegram](https://lobu.ai/platforms/telegram/) · [Discord](https://lobu.ai/platforms/discord/) · [WhatsApp](https://lobu.ai/platforms/whatsapp/) · [Teams](https://lobu.ai/platforms/teams/) · [Google Chat](https://lobu.ai/platforms/google-chat/).

## How Lobu Differs

Lobu is the **infrastructure layer** for autonomous agents. Frameworks like LangChain or CrewAI help you *write* agent logic; Lobu is the delivery layer that runs those agents at scale — sandboxing, persistence, and messaging connectivity.

**vs OpenClaw:** OpenClaw is [single-tenant by design](https://x.com/steipete/status/2026092642623201379) — every user shares the same filesystem and bash session. Lobu keeps the same autonomous loop but runs it **multi-tenant**: one gateway, an isolated sandbox per channel or DM, and org-scoped memory your whole team can share. Full write-up: [lobu.ai/getting-started/comparison](https://lobu.ai/getting-started/comparison/).

| | Lobu | Claude Tag | OpenClaw |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tenancy | Multi-tenant — per-channel/DM isolation | Per-channel @Claude | Single-tenant — one shared runtime |
| Open source / self-host | Yes | No | Yes |
| Model choice | 16 providers | Claude only | Per setup |
| Multi-platform | Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Teams, Google Chat, REST API, MCP | Slack (beta) | [15+ chat platforms](https://openclaw.ai/integrations) |
| Custom connectors / behaviors | Yes (`lobu.config.ts`) | Admin-provisioned tools | Skills + local setup |
| Secrets & network | Gateway proxy, domain-filtered egress | Managed | Direct from agent, no built-in isolation |

## Agent configuration

Runtime configuration is managed through the web app or the same org-scoped REST API used by the CLI. See the [CLI reference](https://lobu.ai/reference/cli/) and [`lobu apply`](https://lobu.ai/reference/lobu-apply/).

```bash
npx @lobu/cli@latest login
npx @lobu/cli@latest org set my-org
npx @lobu/cli@latest agent list
```

Local `lobu.config.ts` projects are still useful for `lobu validate` and `lobu apply` workflows.

## Deployment

The quick start above is the fastest path. For production self-hosting, see the [deployment docs](https://lobu.ai/deployment/docker/): [Docker](https://lobu.ai/deployment/docker/) · [Cloud](https://lobu.ai/deployment/cloud/) · [Kubernetes](https://lobu.ai/deployment/kubernetes/).

## Security and Privacy

Secrets, egress policy, and MCP credential injection stay on the gateway; each channel or DM gets a separate worker subprocess with a best-effort sandbox. Guides: [Security](https://lobu.ai/guides/security/) · [Secret proxy](https://lobu.ai/guides/secret-proxy/) · [Guardrails](https://lobu.ai/guides/guardrails/) · [threat model](docs/SECURITY.md).

- [**Worker egress through the gateway proxy**](https://lobu.ai/guides/security/#network-isolation) — `HTTP_PROXY` on loopback (port from `WORKER_PROXY_PORT`, default 8118) with domain allowlist/blocklist and an optional [LLM egress judge](https://lobu.ai/guides/egress-judge/) for ambiguous hosts. On Linux hosts with an enabled, usable systemd user manager, worker spawn uses `systemd-run --user --scope` with `IPAddressDeny=any` plus `IPAddressAllow=127.0.0.1` and `IPAddressAllow=::1` to permit loopback while blocking non-loopback IP traffic at the kernel; without that scope, including on macOS dev, the proxy is best-effort.
- [**Secrets stay in the gateway**](https://lobu.ai/guides/secret-proxy/) — provider credentials and `${env:}` substitution; OAuth and MCP tokens live in Lobu. Workers get opaque placeholders; the secret proxy swaps real values at egress. Workers never see API keys or refresh tokens.
- [**Threat model**](https://lobu.ai/guides/security/) — `just-bash` and `isolated-vm` are policy + best-effort sandboxes, not security boundaries for hostile code. Read [docs/SECURITY.md](docs/SECURITY.md) before exposing Lobu to untrusted users.
- [**Nix system packages**](docs/SECURITY.md#skills-and-policy) — per-agent reproducible tooling and skill policy via `runtime.nix.packages` and `lobu.config.ts`.

## Support & Consultancy

Lobu is open source, but deploying production-grade agents usually means tuning soul, identity, and integrations. I offer hands-on implementation for:

- **Employee AI assistants** — persistent sandboxed agents on Slack wired into internal tools and docs.
- **Automated customer support** — multi-step ticket handling with human-in-the-loop.
- **Autonomous workflows** — long-running, scheduled background jobs with persistent state.
- **Managed infrastructure** — private Lobu deployments with updates and scaling.
- **Custom tooling & skills** — bespoke MCP servers, Nix runtimes, and agent skills.

I'm a second-time technical founder. Previously founded [rakam.io](https://rakam.io) (enterprise analytics PaaS), acquired by [LiveRamp](https://liveramp.com) (NYSE: RAMP).

> [!TIP]
> Want persistent agents for your team or customers? [Talk to Founder](https://calendar.app.google/LwAk3ecptkJQaYr87) or reach out on [X/Twitter](https://x.com/bu7emba).

result.output:
# Lobu Positioning Analysis

## Main Headline & Subheadline
**Headline:** "Build AI teammates that watch and act."

**Subheadline:** "Build long-running AI teammates that pursue goals, learn from your team, and improve over time."

## Primary Calls-to-Action
1. "Start building" (linked to app.lobu.ai)
2. "Copy setup prompt"
3. "npx @lobu/cli@latest init"

## Positioning Strategy

Lobu emphasizes **composability and flexibility** rather than vendor lock-in. The product positions itself as infrastructure that works *with* existing tools:

- **Open-source foundation:** "Open-source infrastructure for long-running AI teammates...Run it yourself or use Lobu Cloud"
- **Multiple runtime options:** "Local, self-hosted, or managed" with the same codebase
- **Model/connector agnostic:** Supports Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and others; 20+ connectors; swappable sandboxes
- **Framework, not dependency:** "Not hand-rolled scripts. Not a rented employee. An open-source backend...for teammates that watch, remember, and act. Yours to self-host and scope per person."

The positioning avoids suggesting users *must* build on Lobu—instead framing it as "declarative infrastructure you own" that integrates with existing systems, models, and deployment environments.

The onboarding flow is **explicitly agent-centric**. The page opens with "Build and run a Lobu agent" and the quickstart demonstrates creating an agent via CLI initialization.

Regarding alternative use cases: The documentation **does not present a distinct path** for using Lobu purely as a memory or data layer without agent development. content.text:
Short answer: partially, and inconsistently. The claim is true in the code — `lobu memory` + the MCP endpoint genuinely give you your data without running a Lobu agent — but the story is only told properly on one page (`/connect-from/claude/`). Everywhere a new person actually lands, Lobu reads as "a harness you build agents on."

**Where it's already clear**

`/connect-from/claude/` nails it, including the key line: "the same recall is available across Claude, ChatGPT, and your own agents." The landing page hedges toward it via open-source/self-host/model-agnostic framing. And the capability is real — `lobu memory init` detects and wires five clients (claude-code, claude-desktop, codex, gemini-cli, cursor) at `packages/cli/src/commands/memory/_lib/install-targets.ts`, and the wizard offers cloud, localhost, or an arbitrary custom MCP URL.

**The gaps, roughly in order of cost**

The biggest one is that `lobu memory` is invisible outside the CLI itself. It's not in the README once, and the published CLI reference at lobu.ai/reference/cli/ doesn't list it — I checked the live page, and it documents `init`/`run`/`chat`/`call`/`apply` etc. with no memory subcommand. So the docs actively state less than the product does. There's a whole subtree (`memory run`, `memory exec`, `memory health`, `memory seed`, `memory init`, `memory org`) that a reader has no way to discover. That's the cheapest fix available and the one with the best return.

Second, getting-started is single-path. It opens with "Build and run a Lobu agent" and the whole conceptual model is agent-centric — there's no parallel "use Lobu as your memory/data layer, keep your existing agent" entry point. Someone who already has a Claude Code or Cursor setup and doesn't want to switch harnesses has nowhere to start.

Third, the README's framing works against you. Both "two ways in" are Lobu-as-harness: option 1 is scaffold-and-run, option 2 is memory-for-Claude but scoped narrowly as "Memory for Claude Code (and Claude Desktop)" — it undersells to the five clients you actually support plus any MCP client. The architecture diagram shows MCP clients as an inbound arrow to your gateway, which is right, but the surrounding prose never says the quiet part: you can point any MCP client at this and never write a `lobu.config.ts`. The "How Lobu Differs" table is entirely about tenancy and platform breadth — there's no row for anything like "works with your existing agent."

Fourth, and this is more of a strategic tension than a doc bug: the "Capabilities" section argues *against* MCP-as-memory ("Most agent stacks treat MCP as the memory... that knowledge stays siloed"). That's a good argument for the pipeline, but it sits awkwardly next to "connect via MCP and use us as memory." The resolution you already have is the right one — MCP is for *doing*, the graph is for *knowing* — but it's stated inside the agents section, not where a composability-minded reader will hit it.

Fifth, there's no portability/exit story anywhere I could find. For a pitch built on "you own this, it's not lock-in," there's no documented bulk export of the event log or entity graph, and `query_sql` exists but isn't presented as the escape hatch it is.

**What I'd do**

Document `lobu memory` in the CLI reference — that's a pure omission and it's making you look less composable than you are. Then add a third "way in" to the README, framed as bring-your-own-agent rather than Claude-specific, naming all five detected clients and the custom-URL option. A `/connect-from/` index page covering codex, gemini-cli, and cursor alongside Claude would generalize the one page that already works. Longer term, a getting-started fork at the top — "building an agent" vs "adding memory to the agent you have" — is what actually fixes the funnel.

One thing I did not verify: whether a bulk export path exists under some name I didn't grep for. I searched the CLI command registry and the tools directory and found nothing, but I'd treat that as medium confidence rather than settled.

Confidence: high (90) on the CLI/README/docs gaps — I read the registered commands in `packages/cli/src/index.ts`, the install-targets registry, and fetched the live lobu.ai pages. Medium (65) on the export gap, since that's an absence-of-evidence result. Low on anything about app.lobu.ai's in-product onboarding — I didn't look at it, and that's where a lot of first-run positioning actually lands.

Next actions you could pick from:
- Add the `memory` subtree to the CLI reference page (smallest fix, biggest discoverability win)
- Rewrite README section 2 from "Memory for Claude Code" to a bring-your-own-agent framing listing all five clients
- Build a `/connect-from/` index with per-client pages mirroring the Claude one
- Decide whether a documented export path is worth having, given the "yours to own" positioning

content.text:
No, we don't have it that way — it's `lobu memory <subcmd>`, not top-level. `deploy` (aliasing `apply`) is the only alias in the whole CLI. And I owe you a correction: I said `lobu memory` is "invisible outside the CLI itself," but it does have its own **Memory:** section in `lobu --help` (`packages/cli/src/index.ts:132-138`). It's discoverable at the terminal; the gap is only in the published README and CLI reference page.

On your actual question, though — I think the instinct behind it is right, and it sharpens the composability point rather than contradicting it.

The nesting isn't arbitrary. `lobu memory *` routes over MCP JSON-RPC while the top-level commands go through the REST proxy — there's a comment at `index.ts:1055-1057` calling out exactly that split, noting `lobu memory run` and `lobu call` are kept side by side deliberately because they take different paths. So the namespace encodes a real transport boundary.

But that's an internal distinction, and it's leaking into the UX in a way that costs you the exact thing you're asking about. Consider who each verb is for. `lobu apply`, `lobu agent`, `lobu providers`, `lobu sandbox` are all harness-operator commands — they only make sense if you're building on Lobu. The memory verbs are the opposite: `run`, `exec`, `health`, `init` are what a person who *isn't* building on Lobu wants. Those are the composability commands. And they're the ones sitting one level down, behind a noun, in a section at the bottom of help.

The read a newcomer gets from the current tree is that agent-building is the product and memory is a subsystem of it. That's backwards from the pitch. `lobu search "..."` or `lobu query ...` at top level would say "your data is the primary object, the harness is optional" without a word of marketing copy.

Two caveats before you act on that. First, `memory init` and `init` mean genuinely different things — scaffold-a-new-project vs wire-an-existing-agent-to-an-endpoint — so promoting `memory init` to top level collides badly. That one probably wants a different name (`connect`?) rather than a promotion. Second, per your no-back-compat rule, promoting these means moving them, not aliasing them, which is a breaking CLI change and needs a version story.

The narrower version that avoids both problems: promote only the two read verbs a non-Lobu user actually needs — something like `lobu search` and `lobu exec` — and leave `memory org/health/seed/browser-auth` nested as the operator surface they are. That gets the top-level signal without a wholesale reshuffle.

Worth noting the naming ambiguity too: "memory" here spans the MCP transport, the knowledge graph, and the seeding workflow. If you do rework this, that's the moment to pick one meaning.

Confidence: high (92) on the command tree and the single-alias fact — read directly from `index.ts`. High on the transport rationale, which is stated in the source comment, not inferred. The design recommendation is a judgment call, not a verified claim, and I have not checked what `lobu memory` invocations exist in the docs site, skills, or examples — a rename would need that sweep first.

Next actions:
- Grep `skills/`, `examples/`, and the docs repo for `lobu memory` to size the blast radius of any rename
- Decide the narrow promotion (`search`/`exec` only) vs. full reshuffle before touching anything
- Regardless of rename: add the Memory section to the published CLI reference, which is a straight omission today
- Settle what "memory" names — transport, graph, or workflow — since all three currently share it

Full tree from `packages/cli/src/index.ts`. 72 registered commands, 13 top-level groups.

chat <prompt>               Prompt an agent, stream response (--user → Telegram/Slack)

rollback                    Revert a deployment
validate                    Validate config schema, skill IDs, provider config

```

**token**

token revoke <jti>
```

**context** — named API contexts
```

```

**org**
```

```

No — and the answer is more interesting than a yes/no, because the SDK is organized on a completely different principle from the CLI.

**There is no `memory` namespace in the SDK.** The 18 ClientSDK namespaces (`packages/server/src/sandbox/namespaces/`) are flat and domain-named:

```
agents            behaviors         entities          knowledge
conversations     connections       feeds             classifiers
schedules         metrics           notifications     operations
organizations     catalog           auth-profiles     entity-schema
view-templates    action-call
```

So what the CLI calls "memory" is spread across `entities`, `knowledge`, `conversations`, and `feeds` as first-class top-level namespaces. You reach them as `entities.list`, `knowledge.search` — never `memory.entities.list`. That's exactly the shape you were asking about in the CLI: data access at the top level, no noun in front of it.

Which means the CLI's `memory` prefix isn't a modeling decision that runs through the product. It's a CLI-only wrapper around the MCP transport, and `lobu memory exec` is literally sugar for the `run_sdk` tool with a script (`index.ts:1237-1250`). One layer down, the `memory` concept vanishes.

Worth separating two things that are both called "the SDK," because they're unrelated in size:

`@lobu/client` (the published npm package) is nearly empty — `rest`, `sessions`, `createSession`, and two error classes. That's it. It does *not* expose entities/knowledge/search. So an external TypeScript consumer who wants their data has the generated REST client or nothing.

The ClientSDK (18 namespaces, the rich surface) only exists **inside the sandbox**, reachable via `run_sdk`/`query_sdk` over MCP. It's not an importable package.

That's the real finding, and it changes my earlier answer. The composability gap isn't primarily naming — it's that the good data API is only reachable by shipping a script into a sandbox over MCP. There's no `import { entities } from '@lobu/client'`. For "access your data everywhere," MCP clients are well served and the CLI is decently served, but a plain Node/TS program is not.

On aliases specifically, since that's where you were headed: `sdk-aliases.ts` only aliases *field names* within a method (`id`→`entity_id`, `script`→`reaction_script`). There's no method-path or namespace aliasing, so no `memory.*` → `entities.*` bridge exists or could exist through that mechanism.

One nice precedent in that file though — the header notes `search_sdk` renders the alias table into discovery from the same constant the runtime reads, so docs can't drift from behavior. That's the pattern the CLI reference is missing.

You're right, and I was wrong on the substantive claim. Correcting it:

**`@lobu/client` does expose the data surface.** `generated/sdk.gen.ts` has `searchMemory`, `saveMemory`, `readKnowledge`, `manageEntity`, `manageConversations`, `manageFeeds`, plus `querySql`, `querySdk`, `runSdk`, `searchSdk`. It's exported from the package root as the `generated` namespace (`index.ts:1`). So a plain Node/TS program can import and reach entities, knowledge, and search without a sandbox. My "no `import { entities } from '@lobu/client'`" line was wrong — it's `generated.searchMemory(...)`, but the capability is there.

That also dissolves the bigger claim I built on it. The good data API is *not* sandbox-only. It's REST-generated from the same OpenAPI spec that backs the MCP tools.

Now, on consistency — yes, you are, and more than I credited. The pattern holds across all three surfaces:

| | source of truth |
|---|---|
| MCP tools | `search_memory`, `save_memory`, `query_sdk`, `run_sdk`, `query_sql`, `search_sdk` |
| Generated SDK | `searchMemory`, `saveMemory`, `querySdk`, `runSdk`, `querySql`, `searchSdk` |
| CLI | `memory run <tool>` → same tools over MCP JSON-RPC |

That's one tool registry, camelCased by the generator, with the CLI as a thin dispatcher over it. `memory exec` being sugar for `run_sdk` is that consistency showing through, not a shortcut. And "memory" isn't CLI-only vocabulary as I said — `search_memory`/`save_memory` are the actual tool names in the registry, so the CLI group name matches the tools it dispatches.

The 18 `sandbox/namespaces/` are a different layer than I treated them as — the dotted `entities.list` paths reachable *through* `run_sdk`, not a competing top-level API. `run_sdk` is one tool in the registry; the namespaces are its address space. Both consistent, just nested.

So the honest revision: the naming is coherent, and my "SDK doesn't use the memory prefix, so the CLI is inconsistent" was comparing two different layers. What survives from earlier is narrower and all documentation, not architecture — the published CLI reference omits the `memory` group, and `memory browser-auth` sits under memory while doing Chrome/CDP connector setup. That second one is a genuine misfile, but it's one command, not a pattern.

### 2. Bring your own agent — memory over MCP

Point any MCP client at Lobu and it gets durable, structured memory — the same
graph your Lobu agents read. No `lobu.config.ts`, no Lobu runtime.

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http lobu https://lobu.ai/mcp   # or http://localhost:8787/mcp locally
```

Complete the OAuth flow when prompted, then enable the connector. Pair it with a project instruction or skill that tells the agent when to search memory and when to save what it learned.

`lobu memory init` detects and wires the clients you already have —
**Claude Code**, **Claude Desktop**, **Codex**, **Gemini CLI**, and **Cursor** —
or takes a custom MCP URL for anything else. Setup guides:
[Claude](https://lobu.ai/connect-from/claude/) ·
[ChatGPT](https://lobu.ai/connect-from/chatgpt/).

### 3. Your own code — CLI and TypeScript SDK

The data layer is reachable without an agent at all. From the terminal:

```bash
npx @lobu/cli@latest memory run                     # list the memory tools
npx @lobu/cli@latest memory run search_memory '{"query":"onboarding"}'
npx @lobu/cli@latest memory exec ./script.ts        # run a ClientSDK script
```

Or from any Node/TypeScript program, with no sandbox in the loop:

```ts
import { searchMemory, saveMemory, querySql } from "@lobu/client";
```

Every one of these — MCP tools, CLI, and SDK — is generated from the same
server-side tool registry, so the surfaces cannot drift apart.

## Behaviors + external harnesses — investigation

**Behaviors are not missing from MCP. They're reachable, deliberately, through a different door.** The MCP tool list is 11 tools, and `manage_behaviors`/`get_behavior` aren't among them — that's what I flagged earlier. But the design is intentional: `run_sdk`'s own description says "manage Behaviors and feeds," and `search_sdk` uses `'behaviors'` as its worked example with the namespace list injected into the schema. The full `behaviors.*` namespace has 20 methods including `create`, `update`, `trigger`, `setReactionScript`, `submitFeedback`, and `getVersions`.

So the architecture is a **discovery chain**, not a flat tool list: `search_sdk` (find the method) → `query_sdk` (read) / `run_sdk` (write). That's a deliberate trade — 11 stable tools instead of 100+, with the ontology discoverable at runtime. For your data-lake/ontology positioning this is the *right* shape, because the tool list doesn't grow as the ontology does.

**Where it will actually hurt with ChatGPT.** The chain costs a round-trip and requires the client to write a correct TS snippet. Claude handles that well. ChatGPT's connector runtime is weaker at multi-hop tool chaining and at generating code it can't test, so the likely failure isn't "can't reach behaviors" — it's giving up after `search_sdk` or emitting a malformed script. Notably there's **no ChatGPT-specific handling anywhere** in `mcp-handler.ts`; compatibility rides entirely on the generic MCP annotations (the registry cites the OpenAI Apps SDK spec for them). That's clean, but it means nothing is tuned for the weaker client.

**The genuinely good news for your framing:** `behavior_events` is in the SQL-queryable schema. So "what did my behaviors do" is answerable in one hop via `query_sql`, no code generation and no chain. For read/reporting — which is most of what an external agent wants — the path already exists and is single-hop. It just isn't advertised as the behaviors story.

**My read, given "connect their agents, we do the ontology":** don't add behavior CRUD to MCP. Writes belong to whoever owns the behavior; external agents mostly need to *read and reason*. The cheap high-leverage move is making the single-hop read path obvious — surfacing `behavior_events` in the `query_sql` description, and giving `search_sdk` a nudge toward it for behavior queries. That's a description change, not new surface area.

Caveat: this is all static reading. I have **not** driven a real ChatGPT connector against it, so "ChatGPT will struggle with the chain" is a reasoned prediction from how its runtime behaves, not something I measured here. Worth an actual live test before you build on it.

Confidence: high (90) on the behaviors mechanics — read the registry, the namespace, `search_sdk`, and the queryable schema. Medium (60) on the ChatGPT prediction, untested. High that the README/SDK edits are accurate, since I verified every command form and export name against source; not yet verified they build.

**No API changes in this PR** — confirmed. Two files, one additive re-export plus README prose. The tool registry is untouched, so the OpenAPI spec and MCP tool list are unchanged.

**Why you see events but no conversation for ChatGPT**

`sourceContext` — which is what carries `conversationId` — is only ever constructed in one place: `workspace/multi-tenant.ts:328`, on the worker path, with `clientId: 'lobu-worker'`, populated from a worker run token that already knows its platform/channel/conversation. The comment at `mcp-handler.ts:940` says it outright: "worker-originated source conversation is per request."

An external MCP client like ChatGPT authenticates via OAuth, not a worker run token. It never gets a `sourceContext`, so `ctx.sourceContext?.conversationId` is `null`. Following that through `resolveRunInitiator` (`tools/initiator.ts:40-50`): with no `agentId` and no worker context, a ChatGPT caller falls to the `userId` branch — `initiatorKind: 'user'`, `initiatorRef: { user_id }`, and **no conversation_id at all**.

So the writes land in `events` (which is why you see the logs), but nothing creates or attributes a conversation row. There's no ChatGPT conversation to show in Recent because one was never created. `save_content.ts:351` corroborates this — its comment distinguishes the worker-originated session "carries team + channel in sourceContext" from other callers.

This is a structural gap, not a display bug. Fixing it means minting a conversation identity for OAuth MCP sessions — the MCP session ID is the natural candidate, since `mcp-handler.ts` already tracks session continuity per user/agent and even handles the gateway reusing one upstream session across turns. That's a real design decision though: what counts as a "conversation" for a stateless-ish MCP client, and whether a long-lived ChatGPT connector session should be one conversation or many.

That's clearly a separate PR from this one, and it's the more interesting of the two threads — it's the same "external harnesses as first-class" concern, one layer deeper than the README.

Confidence: high (90) on the mechanism — single construction site, single assignment site, and the initiator branching all read directly. Medium (60) on "nothing else creates a conversation for MCP callers"; I traced `sourceContext` exhaustively but did not audit `manage_conversations` for an independent creation path, which would be the thing that falsifies this.

Next:
- Check `tools/admin/manage_conversations.ts` for an independent creation path before treating the gap as confirmed
- Commit/push this PR — it's settled and gate-clean, and unrelated to the conversation gap
- Scope the MCP-conversation-identity PR: decide whether an MCP session maps to one conversation or many
- Still worth the live ChatGPT connector test, which would show both the behaviors chain and this gap in one pass

content.text:
That refines the picture in an important way. Correcting my previous answer:

**There IS a conversation-creation path for MCP callers** — `manage_conversations` with `action: send`. It derives a conversation id from the caller's own `userId` via `buildApiConversationId` when no explicit id is passed, stamps `channelId = api_<userId>`, and creates it under `platform: "web"`. So my "no conversation is ever created for an MCP caller" was too strong.

But it doesn't rescue the ChatGPT case, for two reasons.

First, `manage_conversations` lives in `ADMIN_TOOLS` (`tools/admin/index.ts:172`), not `AGENT_TOOLS` — so it isn't in the 11-tool MCP list a ChatGPT connector sees. Reaching it requires `run_sdk` with a `conversations.*` script, which is the same multi-hop chain problem as behaviors.

Second, and more decisive: that path only creates a conversation when someone *sends a turn through Lobu* — it enqueues a message for a Lobu agent to answer. That's not what ChatGPT is doing. ChatGPT is calling `search_memory`/`save_memory` as a tool, with the conversation living in ChatGPT's own UI. Nothing in that flow goes through `send`.

So the corrected diagnosis: the events land (which is what you're seeing), and `resolveRunInitiator` attributes them to `initiatorKind: 'user'` with no `conversation_id`, because `sourceContext` is worker-only. There's no bug — the conversation genuinely doesn't exist on our side. What's missing is a notion of "an external MCP client's session is a conversation," and `platform: "web"` + `api_<userId>` channel is the closest existing shape to build it on.

That's still a separate PR, and now better specified: it needs a `platform` value for external MCP clients (ChatGPT isn't "web"), and a decision on whether one OAuth connector session maps to one conversation or many.

**This PR:** `review-fix` finished, exit 0, and edited both files. Its changes were all corrections to real errors of mine — the `memory init` capability claim (auto-config vs. manual instructions differ per client), the `memory exec` example (my `./script.ts` placeholder replaced with a valid inline script), and the "cannot drift apart" overclaim. I still need to re-verify the tree it produced before committing, since it wrote code I haven't checked.

Confidence: high (90) on the corrected mechanism — read the send path, the admin-tool registration, and the initiator branching directly. Higher than my last answer, which overstated the gap by missing this path entirely. Still medium on whether some non-`sourceContext` route stamps conversation ids elsewhere; I've now checked the two most likely places.

Next:
- Re-verify post-review-fix tree (exports + new snippet), then commit, push, open PR, `make review` once
- MCP-conversation PR now needs: a platform value for external clients, plus session→conversation cardinality
- A live ChatGPT connector run would confirm both this and the behaviors chain in one pass

I have what I need. Let me answer the fan-out question first, since it gates the plan.

## Do we need to fan out?

No — and I'd push back on it for this specific work. Reading these five files took a handful of targeted greps, and the answer changed twice along the way. Every error I've made in this session came from asserting without reading; subagents would multiply that risk, not reduce it, because I'd be grading their claims instead of the code. Per your own rule, subagents are for read-only breadth where I don't know where to look. Here I now do.

The one place fan-out earns its keep is later: if the plan produces genuinely independent implementation slices (server attribution vs. frontend rendering), those can go to separate worktrees in parallel. Not before the design is settled.

## What I found — the gap is narrower than "Recent doesn't show MCP"

`Recent` is fed by `useRecentAgentThreads` (`agents.ts:514`), which fans out per-agent to `GET /history/threads?scope=all`. That `scope=all` **already widens across platforms** — the server comment at `agent-history.ts:608` says exactly "every conversation for the agent across platforms (Slack, Telegram, …)". And `agent-thread-list.ts` derives `platform` from the conversation-id prefix, with per-platform visibility filtering already built.

So the rendering path is not the problem. **Slack should already appear in Recent.** If it doesn't for you, that's a distinct bug — most likely the ACL gate in `filterChannelsForRequester`, or the agent not being bound to the channel — and it needs reproducing before it gets designed around.

The MCP gap is upstream and is the one I traced earlier: `sourceContext` is worker-only (`multi-tenant.ts:328`, `clientId: 'lobu-worker'`), so an OAuth MCP caller produces `initiatorKind: 'user'` with `conversation_id: null`. No conversation row is created, so there's nothing for `listAgentThreads` to return. The events land; the conversation never exists.

## Plan

**Phase 0 — reproduce, before any code.** Two separate checks: does a Slack thread actually show in Recent today (and if not, why — ACL, binding, or missing row)? And confirm live that a ChatGPT `save_memory` call leaves events with no conversation. This is the step that decides whether Slack is even in scope. I'd want to do this against a real org before writing anything.

**Phase 1 — MCP session → conversation identity (server).** The design decisions, which are genuinely yours:
- **Platform value.** ChatGPT isn't `"web"`. Options: one `"mcp"` platform, or per-client (`"chatgpt"`, `"claude"`) from the MCP `clientInfo`. Per-client is better for the UI and costs little, since `clientInfo` arrives at initialize.
- **Cardinality.** One OAuth connector session = one conversation, or one per turn? The handler already tracks session continuity and notes the gateway reuses upstream sessions across turns, so session-scoped is feasible — but a months-long ChatGPT connector session becoming one infinite conversation is probably wrong. Likely wants a rolling window.
- Mint `sourceContext` for OAuth MCP callers so `resolveRunInitiator` produces `initiatorKind: 'agent_session'` with a real `conversation_id`, reusing `buildApiConversationId`'s shape.

**Phase 2 — visibility + rendering.** Confirm the new platform passes `filterChannelsForRequester` (a new platform with no ACL rows may fail closed — that's the likeliest trap), and give it an icon/label in the sidebar.

**Phase 3 — verify.** Live: connect ChatGPT, call a memory tool, see it in Recent. Plus Slack from Phase 0.

Phases 1 and 2 are one concern and should be one PR. Phase 0 gates all of it.

Two things I'd flag as unresolved rather than assumed: whether Slack is actually broken (I have no evidence either way — your report is the only signal, and it contradicts the code), and the ACL behavior for a novel platform, which I inferred from the fail-closed pattern but did not read.

Confidence: high (88) on the Recent data path — traced hook → endpoint → service. High (90) on the MCP attribution gap, now traced twice. **Low on the Slack claim** — the code says it should work, so I'd treat "Slack should be shown" as needing reproduction first, not implementation.

Next:
- Tell me whether Slack genuinely doesn't appear, and I'll reproduce it — that materially changes scope
- Decide platform value (per-client vs. generic `"mcp"`) and session cardinality; both are design calls I shouldn't make alone
- The composability PR is still uncommitted and gate-clean — worth landing before starting this
- Live ChatGPT connector run would settle Phase 0's second half and the behaviors chain together

content.text:
Now I can explain this concretely.

## The question

When ChatGPT (or Claude Code) calls `save_memory` five times over three days, how many rows should show up in Recent — one, three, or five?

Every other platform answers this for free because the platform itself defines a boundary:

- **Slack** — `thread_ts`. A thread is a conversation. Natural, user-visible, ends on its own.
- **Web** — the packed id from `buildApiConversationId`. With a `threadId` you get a distinct conversation; without one you get `{agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}` — a single stable id per user per agent, forever.

MCP has **no equivalent signal**. There's no thread, no channel, no "conversation ended" event. ChatGPT holds one OAuth connector session open for weeks. So you have to invent the boundary, and whatever you pick is what Recent shows.

## The three options

**One conversation, forever.** Reuse the no-`threadId` shape: one row per (user, agent, client). ChatGPT is one entry in Recent that keeps updating. Simplest — it's the existing web fallback, already proven. But that row grows unbounded, and its title is whatever the first message was, so a months-old title sits atop today's activity.

**One per MCP session.** Boundary = the MCP session lifetime, which `mcp-handler.ts` already tracks. Semantically the most honest. The problem I flagged earlier: the handler notes the gateway may reuse one upstream session across turns, and a ChatGPT connector session can persist for weeks — so in practice this often collapses into option 1 anyway, but unpredictably. Same outcome, less control.

**Rolling idle window.** New conversation after N minutes/hours of inactivity from that client. Matches how people actually think — "my ChatGPT session this morning" vs. "yesterday's." Recent stays readable and titles stay fresh. Costs a `last_activity` check on each write and one arbitrary constant.

## What I'd recommend

The idle window, with a long timeout — a few hours. Reasoning: Recent is a *navigation* surface. Its job is "take me back to the thing I was doing." Option 1 fails that at scale because one ever-growing row can't be navigated back into meaningfully. Option 2 gives you the same failure but non-deterministically, which is worse to debug.

A few hours is long enough that a working session stays one conversation, short enough that distinct days separate. And it degrades gracefully: if you pick wrong, changing a constant is cheap, whereas migrating conversation identity later is not.

The one thing I'd genuinely defer to you on is the constant. It's a product feel question — do you want ChatGPT usage to read as "a session" or "a running relationship with the agent?" If the former, hours. If the latter, option 1 is honest and simpler, and you should take it.

## Guidance on sequencing

Whatever you pick, I'd still do the ACL check first. If `filterChannelsForRequester` fails closed for a platform with no channel rows, MCP conversations won't render regardless of how you slice them — and that would invalidate the cardinality work before it starts. It's a single file read.

One caveat on my recommendation: I'm reasoning about how Recent *should* feel, not from usage data. If you have signal on how people actually use the ChatGPT connector — bursty vs. continuous — that beats my inference.

Confidence: high (92) on the mechanics — read the id builder, its header, and Slack's working path. The recommendation is a judgment call, explicitly not verified against usage.

Next:
- Pick cardinality (my rec: idle window, few hours; option 1 if you want simplest)
- Read `filterChannelsForRequester` for the no-channel-rows case — gates everything

That means option 2 and option 3 are the same option. I presented them as a trade-off; they aren't. The session id *is* the rolling idle window, with the timeout already chosen at 1 hour and already implemented, persisted, and multi-replica correct.

The corrected design: **map conversation identity to the MCP session id.** No new boundary logic, no new constant, no `last_activity` bookkeeping. One thing to verify before building: whether 1 hour is right as a *conversation* boundary. It's currently tuned for auth/session hygiene, and those goals can diverge — a user returning after 90 minutes gets a new conversation, which may or may not be what you want in Recent. The single writer is `message-consumer.ts:465`, on the path that processes an agent *turn*. `search_memory`, `save_memory`, `query_sql`, `query_sdk`, `run_sdk` — none of them touch a queue producer (grepped: zero hits across `search.ts`, `save_content.ts`, `execute.ts`). That settles it definitively. Six FKs point at `oauth_clients`, including `events.client_id` and `mcp_sessions.client_id`.

## No — don't consolidate. They're not the same layer.

The question is worth asking, but the tables aren't redundant. `oauth_clients` is **OAuth 2.1 protocol infrastructure**, not a UI convenience:

```
events.client_id                    → oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
mcp_sessions.client_id              → oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
oauth_tokens.client_id              → oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
oauth_authorization_codes.client_id → oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
oauth_device_codes.client_id        → oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
```

Deleting that layer means deleting Dynamic Client Registration, token issuance, the device-code flow (which is how ChatGPT authenticates), and revocation. The `/clients` UI listing is a thin read over it — `client-routes.ts:313` joins `oauth_clients` to `oauth_tokens` to compute connected/authorized state. The UI is the byproduct, not the purpose.

**The three layers are genuinely distinct, and each has a different lifetime:**

- `oauth_clients` — identity and authorization. Lives months. `codex-mcp-client` is still registered from July 14. Revoking it kills access.
- `mcp_sessions` — a connection. Lives ≤1 hour idle. Says "who is talking right now."
- `conversations` — a unit of work someone navigates back to. Lives as long as it's useful.

Slack has exactly the same three (installation / socket connection / thread) and nobody would collapse those. Consolidating would mean either giving conversations FK duty for token revocation, or making OAuth registrations carry sidebar titles. Both are worse.

**So yes, we need the layer — but the *specific* thing missing is small.** One `upsertConversation` call on the MCP tool path, keyed by session id, `kind: "owned"`, `platform: "mcp"`. Everything else already exists: identity (`oauth_clients.client_name` — `openai-mcp`, `claude-code`), boundary (session TTL), and rendering (the Slack path I verified live).

Where I'd push back on the framing: the instinct that something is over-layered is right, it's just aimed at the wrong seam. The genuinely confusing thing is that `conversations` is written in exactly one place — the queue consumer — so anything not going through a queued *turn* silently has no listing. That's the coupling worth loosening, and it's the same fix as above. The real consolidation opportunity is "one function materializes a conversation, called from every origin," not "delete a table."

content.text:
That's the confirming detail. Here's the picture.

## The actual architectural problem

`conversations` is described in its own migration as "the single sidebar source," but it isn't. The thread list has **two** sources:

1. `conversations` rows — written in exactly one place, `message-consumer.ts:465`, on queued turns
2. A **regex over conversation-id strings** — `regexp_match(conversation_id, '_watcher_([0-9]+)_run_')` (`agent-thread-list.ts:266`), reverse-parsing behavior runs at query time

So behaviors never materialize rows; they're recovered by pattern-matching ids. That's the same shape as the MCP gap — an origin that doesn't flow through the queue has to be special-cased downstream. Two origins already need it. MCP would be the third.

That's the real issue, and it's why I'd resist framing the MCP work as a patch. The invariant "every conversation has a row" is stated but not enforced, and each new origin either gets forgotten (MCP: invisible) or bolted on as a query-time parser (behaviors: string regex, which breaks the moment an id format changes).

## Target shape

**One materialization seam, called by every origin.** `upsertConversation` is already the right function — idempotent upsert on the natural PK, `GREATEST` on activity, `COALESCE` so late-arriving titles don't clobber, errors swallowed so listing never breaks a live turn. It's built for exactly this. The defect is that only one caller uses it.

The end state:

- Every origin calls it at its own boundary: queue turns (already), MCP tool execution (session id), direct API, behavior runs.
- `agent-thread-list.ts` becomes a plain read of `conversations`. The watcher regex goes away — behaviors write a real row with `platform: "behavior"` and `behaviorId` as a column instead of something parsed out of a string.
- `classifyConversation` becomes the single place origin→`(kind, platform)` is decided, rather than each caller guessing.

The payoff is that conversation identity stops being encoded in id *strings* that downstream code parses. Right now the id carries semantics — `_watcher_<id>_run_`, the packed web tuple, `slack:C…:ts` — and three different places know how to decode it. That's the coupling generating this whole class of bug.

## How to get there

Order matters, and it's incremental rather than a big refactor:

**First**, MCP calls `upsertConversation` — the gap you have now, small and self-contained. This also validates that a non-queue origin can call the seam cleanly, which is the assumption everything else rests on.

**Second**, behaviors write real rows, with the regex kept as a fallback read. Backfill from existing ids. Once rows exist for all live behaviors, delete the regex. This is the risky one — it needs the read path to tolerate both sources during migration, which the `COALESCE`/`GREATEST` upsert makes safe.

**Third**, audit remaining origins (direct API, device workers) for the same silence, and make `agent-thread-list` a pure table read.

Each step is independently shippable and independently revertible. Nothing requires a coordinated cutover.

What I'd *not* do: introduce a new abstraction over `upsertConversation`, or move materialization into a trigger. The function is fine; the problem is call sites. And per your rule about deletion needing structural evidence, the watcher regex only goes once real rows demonstrably cover the same set — that's a verifiable condition, not a judgment call.

One caveat: I've traced the queue, MCP, and behavior origins, but not audited every writer of `agent_transcript_snapshot` or the device-worker path. There may be a fourth origin I haven't seen, which would add to step three without changing the shape.

Confidence: high (90) on the two-source diagnosis — read both the single upsert call site and the regex. High on `upsertConversation` being the right seam, read in full. Medium (65) on step two's difficulty; I haven't checked how many behavior conversation ids exist or whether the backfill is clean.

Next:
- Step one is also the fix you already need — worth starting there regardless of whether you buy the longer arc
- Land the composability PR first; it's uncommitted, gate-clean, and unrelated
- Before step two: count behavior conversation ids in prod to size the backfill
- Still open and cheap: the `query_sql` silent-empty trap

Teammate dispatched with both your requirements built in as hard constraints. Now the policy question.

## The policy question

`conversations` rows are written by exactly one call site — `message-consumer.ts:465`, on a queued agent *turn*. MCP memory tools never enqueue anything, so they never produce a row. To fix that, something has to call `upsertConversation` on the MCP path. The policy question is: **on which calls?**

It matters because Recent is a navigation surface with roughly 8 visible slots (`useRecentAgentThreads` defaults to `limit: 8`). Whatever policy you pick decides what occupies them.

**Option A — every MCP tool call.** Any `search_memory` materializes a conversation. Maximally complete, and genuinely bad in practice: a behavior or background agent polling memory on a tight interval would produce a row per session and evict everything human-relevant from those 8 slots. Reads are also the overwhelming majority of MCP traffic.

**Option B — writes only** (`save_memory`, `run_sdk`, and the mutating admin tools). A conversation appears when the client *changed something*. Recent stays a log of what was done, which matches what it shows today — every existing entry is a turn that produced work. The gap: a long ChatGPT session that only reads leaves no trace, even though real work happened from the user's point of view.

**Option C — first call of a session, any kind.** One row per MCP session regardless of read/write. Since sessions already expire after 1 hour idle (`SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS`, `mcp-handler.ts:52`), this naturally means "one Recent entry per working session per client." Bounded by construction — a polling agent that reconnects hourly produces at most 24 rows/day, and a chatty session produces exactly one.

I lean **C**, with a caveat. It's the closest analogue to what Recent already means for the other platforms: a Slack thread appears because someone engaged, not because the agent wrote something. C treats an MCP session the same way — engagement, not mutation. And it inherits the session TTL rather than inventing a new constant, which is the part that made me revise my earlier answer to you.

The caveat is the title. `conversations.title` comes from `data.messageText?.slice(0, 200)` — the user's message. An MCP session has no message text; the first tool call is `search_memory` with a query string, or `save_memory` with content. So C needs a title source, and the honest options are the first tool's query/content, or a synthesized one ("ChatGPT session, 14:32"). That's a real sub-decision and it's where C is weakest — B at least has content to title from.

Where I'd genuinely defer to you: whether a read-only ChatGPT session *should* show in Recent. If your mental model is "Recent = things the agent did," B is correct and C is noise. If it's "Recent = places I was working," C is correct and B loses real sessions. I don't think there's a technically-right answer — it depends what you want the sidebar to be.

One thing I'd avoid regardless: making this configurable. A policy knob here means two behaviors to reason about and neither gets tested properly.

Confidence: high (90) on the mechanics behind the options — traced the single writer, the session TTL, and the `limit: 8` default. The recommendation is a product judgment, not a verified claim, and I have no usage data on read/write ratios per MCP client to back it.

**Every MCP tool call already writes an audit event:**

```json

```

1,222 in 7 days, 1,022 with `client_id`. So attribution isn't missing — it's complete and already flowing. What's missing is only the *listing row* that Recent reads.

**This changes the policy question in two ways.**

First, it removes the title problem that made me hedge on option C. I said an MCP session has no message text to title from — wrong. The audit trail carries `tool_name` per call, so a session can be titled from what it actually did ("query_sql, search_memory — 14:17"), or from the first meaningful tool's arguments. No synthesized placeholder needed.

Second, and more usefully: since the audit events already exist with `client_id` and timestamps, **the conversation row can be derived rather than written at call time.** That's the same trick `agent-thread-list.ts` already does for behaviors — except over a real indexed column (`client_id`, `created_at`) instead of a regex over id strings. That said, I'd still write the row rather than derive it. Deriving is what created the two-source problem I flagged as the architectural issue — it works until the grouping logic and the writer disagree. The audit events are better used as the *backfill source*: you can materialize conversation rows for MCP sessions that already happened, which means Recent isn't empty on day one. That's a real advantage the other options didn't have.

That's a genuine gap — either MCP sessions need an agent binding (the handler does track `requestedAgentId`), or the PK doesn't fit this case. I'd want that resolved before writing code, since it's a schema-level constraint rather than a policy choice.

This is the decisive detail. All three readers filter by `agent_id = ${agentId}` — an equality predicate. Under SQL semantics, `agent_id = 'x'` never matches NULL, so nullable rows would be **invisible to every existing reader**, silently.

Here's my answer.

## Not 3 — and not because of migration cost

Option 3 is the semantically honest model, and I'd normally agree with your instinct. But the three readers all filter `WHERE agent_id = ${agentId}`. NULL never satisfies equality, so nullable MCP rows would be silently invisible to all of them — the sidebar, the sandbox pin lookup, and the single-conversation fetch. You'd ship a migration and still see nothing in Recent, with no error anywhere. Every one of those call sites would need `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` or a separate agentless query path, plus the PK rework. That's a lot of surface to get exactly right for a case that, I'd argue, isn't actually agentless.

**The something-else I'd recommend: bind the session to a real agent at connect time, and make that binding explicit rather than optional.**

The premise that MCP sessions have no agent is a current-state artifact, not a fact about the domain. `mcp-handler.ts` already tracks `requestedAgentId` from both the `x-lobu-agent-id` header and `clientInfo.agentId`. The `/mcp/{slug}` scoped endpoint exists. 9% of sessions already bind. What's missing is a *default* for the other 91% — not a schema hole.

So: when an MCP session initializes without an explicit agent, resolve it to the org's system/builder agent, which already exists per org and is exactly the "this org's general-purpose agent" concept. That gives you:

- No migration, no nullable PK column, no magic sentinel value every consumer must learn.
- The existing readers work unchanged — `agent_id = ${agentId}` matches.
- A real navigable target. Clicking the Recent entry lands somewhere meaningful.
- The upgrade path is natural: as more clients bind explicitly, they simply move off the default.

You raised the objection to this yourself in the option text — it conflates "ChatGPT talked to my org" with "the builder did work." That's real, but it's solved by `platform: "mcp"` plus the client title, which you're already getting. The row reads as "ChatGPT · 14:32" under the builder agent, not as builder activity. `platform` carries the distinction; `agent_id` just needs to be a valid FK-ish target for grouping.

The one thing I'd verify before building: that every org actually has a system agent. `lobu-crm` showed `lobu-builder` and `lobu-team` had one too, so it looks universal — but if an org can exist without one, the default has no target and you're back to the sentinel.

**On your listing choice** — one row per session — that composes cleanly with this. Conversation id from the MCP session id, `platform: "mcp"`, `kind: "owned"` (it's user-owned, not a shared channel), agent = explicit-or-system-default, title from the audit trail's `tool_name` sequence, boundary from the existing 1-hour TTL. And the 7 days of audit events give you a backfill so Recent isn't empty on day one.

Where I'd genuinely still defer: if you think org-scoped-agentless is a first-class concept you'll want elsewhere too — org-level memory, org-level policy, sessions that deliberately aren't any agent's — then option 3 is right and the migration is worth doing properly, including fixing those three readers. My recommendation assumes MCP sessions are the only agentless case. If they're the first of several, pay the cost now.

Confidence: high (90) on the NULL-invisibility problem — read all three readers, all use equality. Medium (70) on system-agent-as-default being universally available; saw it in two orgs, didn't verify it's guaranteed.

- Otherwise I'll verify every org has a system agent, then build: session-id conversation, `platform: "mcp"`, system-agent default, audit-derived title

**Why it simplifies things, concretely:**

No migration. `agent_id` stays `NOT NULL` and stays in the PK. - **title** — from the audit trail's `tool_name` sequence

That's the blocker, and it's decisive. Here's what the dig turned up.

## The admin gate is fine. A different thing isn't.

**Admin gate: not a problem.** I traced it fully. A non-owner doesn't get rejected — they get `allowNotGraphed: false` (`agent-history.ts:552-557`), which only flows into `filterChannelsForRequester` over **bound channel rows**. That path exists solely for `kind: "platform"` conversations. `kind: "owned"` skips it entirely (`agent-thread-list.ts:203`). So the concern I flagged last turn is resolved: our MCP rows, being `owned`, never touch the channel ACL. The chat-route admin gate at `agent.ts:510` is a separate route and doesn't apply here.

**The actual blocker.** `kind: "owned"` rows are filtered through `webThreadIdFromConversationId`:

```
const prefix = `${agentId}_${userId}_${organizationId}_`;
if (!conversationId.startsWith(prefix)) return null;
```

and the caller does `if (!threadId || ...) continue;` — **skip the row**.

So an `owned` conversation whose id isn't the packed web format is silently dropped from the listing. If I use the MCP session id as `conversation_id` with `kind: "owned"`, the row will be written correctly, satisfy every ACL check, and then be **discarded at render time** with no error. Exactly the failure mode I warned about for nullable `agent_id`, reached by a different route.

This is the same root cause as the behaviors regex: conversation identity encoded in id *strings* that downstream code parses. Third instance now.

**Three ways out, and I'd take the second:**

Make the MCP conversation id conform to the packed prefix — `{agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}_mcp-{sessionId}`. Zero changes to the read path; it just works. This is what the `mcp-personal-mrtp7yl5` row I found earlier already does, which is why *that* one renders. Downside: perpetuates string-encoded identity.

Give MCP its own branch in the listing loop, keyed on `platform === "mcp"` rather than falling into the `owned` web-parsing branch. Slightly more code, but it stops the id from carrying semantics and is the first step of the architectural cleanup I proposed — the same shape behaviors will eventually need.

Change `kind` to `"platform"` so it takes the other branch. Rejected: that subjects MCP rows to channel ACL, and there are no channel rows for them, so they'd fail closed.

I'd go with the second — one explicit branch, no parsing — and use the first as the fallback if you want the absolute minimum diff. Either is small; they differ in whether you're paying down the coupling or adding to it.

Confidence: high (92) — traced the gate through all three fallthrough branches, read the parser and its caller. This is verified, not inferred, and it changes the design I gave you last turn (which assumed `owned` + session id would just work).

Next:

- Then I'll build it — everything else in the design is settled

Now I can see what the parse is actually *for*, and it changes the answer.

## What the parse is doing

`webThreadIdFromConversationId` isn't validation. It's **extracting the routing key**. Look at the two branches:

- `owned` → `id: threadId` (the *suffix*, stripped of the `{agentId}_{userId}_{org}_` prefix)
- `platform` → `id: row.conversationId` (the whole id)

They emit different `id` values because the frontend routes on them differently — a web thread navigates by thread id, a platform conversation by full conversation id. The parse exists to recover a field that was never stored: **the routable id**.

Note the `platform` branch already got the lesson. Its comment says the label comes "from the EXPLICIT stored platform, not by parsing the id," because parsing mislabelled gchat's `spaces_A_threads_B` as web. Someone already fixed the *platform* half of this bug by adding a column. The *routable id* half is still parsed.

## So: what's actually best

Store the routable id as a column instead of deriving it. `thread_id text` (nullable — NULL means "the whole conversation_id is the route"), populated at write time by whoever knows the answer. The listing loop becomes:

```
id: row.threadId ?? row.conversationId
```

No parsing, no branch on `kind`, no skip-on-parse-failure. MCP writes its session id as `conversation_id` with `thread_id = null` and renders correctly with zero special-casing. Behaviors eventually do the same, and the `_watcher_<id>_run_` regex dies too — it's the identical defect.

That's the long-term answer, and it's the same move the `platform` column already made. It's also small: one nullable column, one backfill (the parse rule *is* the backfill query), and deletions at three call sites.

## Ranking, honestly

**Conform the id** — a workaround. It makes MCP masquerade as a web conversation so an unrelated parser accepts it. It'd work, and it's what the existing `mcp-personal-…` row accidentally does. But it encodes "MCP session" inside a string shaped like something else, and the next reader of that id has to know the trick.

**The `platform === "mcp"` branch** — not a workaround, but not the fix either. A third branch emitting a third id convention. It solves MCP and leaves behaviors broken, so you'd be back here.

**The `thread_id` column** — the actual fix. Removes the class rather than the instance, which is what your own AGENTS.md asks for on a root cause seen more than once. This is the third instance in this session.

If you want MCP shipped this week and the cleanup later, take the branch — it's forward-compatible with the column and doesn't need undoing. I'd resist conforming the id, because that one *does* need undoing.

One caveat: I've read the two consumers in this loop, but not every frontend consumer of the returned `id`. Adding the column is safe; *changing* what `id` contains for existing web threads would not be, so the backfill must reproduce the current parse exactly.

-- migrate:up

-- Immutable per-conversation sandbox pin. On a conversation's FIRST turn, freeze
-- the RESOLVED runtime selection (which provider + which environment's creds
-- execute this conversation's sandbox). Every later turn reads the pin instead of
-- re-resolving the agent's CURRENT environment — so an admin repointing
-- agents.environment_id never moves an existing conversation's sandbox
-- (one-conversation-one-sandbox), while new conversations pick up the new realm.
--
-- Why freeze the RESOLVED value, not a reference:
--  - The sandbox filesystem name is already conversation-stable
--    (sha256(org:agent:conversation), no provider in it — vercel.ts), so the pin
--    is a (provider, creds)-routing concern, not an FS one.
--  - We store the resolved mode + provider + environment id, NOT the secret
--    (creds rotate live behind the same environment id — desirable) and NOT the
--    tri-state "unset/deployment_default" marker (that would re-read the mutable
--    LOBU_RUNTIME_PROVIDER and could migrate a live conversation's FS). The
--    unset case is resolved down to a concrete mode ('builtin' local just-bash,
--    or 'provider' + provider id) and frozen.
--  - No FK to environments: it is hard-deleted (no deleted_at). A pinned env that
--    is later deleted/deactivated must FAIL CLOSED (matches PR-0), not dangle to
--    system creds — enforced in app code (resolveRuntimeCredentials: an env-bound
--    resolution never splices system env), not by a cascade.
--
-- Provider selection is SOLELY the agent's Environment. The deployment-wide
-- LOBU_RUNTIME_PROVIDER env var is intentionally NOT consulted: it only ever
-- named a provider KIND while credentials always come from the environments
-- vault, so it could never route a working sandbox on its own. INTENDED BREAKING
-- CHANGE: a self-host that set LOBU_RUNTIME_PROVIDER expecting remote bash (with
-- no Environment attached) now runs local just-bash — attach a provider
-- Environment to the agent instead.
--
-- sandbox_provider_id doubles as the "pinned yet?" guard: NULL = unpinned, and
-- the first-turn CAS is `... WHERE sandbox_provider_id IS NULL` for mode
-- 'provider'. Because 'builtin' has a NULL provider id too, sandbox_mode carries
-- the pinned/unpinned bit: NULL sandbox_mode = unpinned.
ALTER TABLE public.conversations
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS sandbox_mode         text,   -- NULL=unpinned; 'builtin' | 'provider'
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS sandbox_provider_id  text,   -- runtimeProviderId when mode='provider'
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS sandbox_environment_id text, -- environments.id backing the provider creds (NULL for builtin)
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS sandbox_pinned_at    timestamptz;

-- ADD CONSTRAINT has no IF NOT EXISTS in Postgres; guard each on pg_constraint
-- so the up migration is idempotent (a partial-failure rerun won't duplicate-
-- object error), matching the ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS above.
DO $$
BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'conversations_sandbox_mode_check'
  ) THEN
    ALTER TABLE public.conversations
      ADD CONSTRAINT conversations_sandbox_mode_check
        CHECK (sandbox_mode IS NULL OR sandbox_mode IN ('builtin', 'provider'));
  END IF;

  -- mode='provider' requires a provider id; mode='builtin' must not carry one.
  IF NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'conversations_sandbox_provider_consistent'
  ) THEN
    ALTER TABLE public.conversations
      ADD CONSTRAINT conversations_sandbox_provider_consistent
        CHECK (
          (sandbox_mode = 'provider' AND sandbox_provider_id IS NOT NULL)
          OR (sandbox_mode = 'builtin' AND sandbox_provider_id IS NULL)
          OR (sandbox_mode IS NULL AND sandbox_provider_id IS NULL)
        );
  END IF;
END $$;

-- migrate:down
-- squawk-ignore ban-drop-column -- rollback path for columns introduced by this migration
ALTER TABLE public.conversations
  DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS conversations_sandbox_provider_consistent,
  DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS conversations_sandbox_mode_check,
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS sandbox_pinned_at,
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS sandbox_environment_id,
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS sandbox_provider_id,
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS sandbox_mode;

-- migrate:up

-- Store the ROUTABLE id explicitly instead of re-deriving it by parsing
-- `conversation_id` at read time.
--
-- The listing loop (agent-thread-list.ts) emitted two different `id` values:
--   kind='owned'    -> the SUFFIX of the packed web id, recovered by
--                      webThreadIdFromConversationId() stripping the
--                      `{agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}_` prefix
--   kind='platform' -> the whole conversation_id
-- The frontend routes on that `id` (a web thread by threadId, a platform
-- conversation by conversationId), so the parse was reconstructing a field that
-- was simply never stored.
--
-- Parsing the id string is the same defect the `platform` column already fixed:
-- that column exists precisely because deriving the label from the id mislabelled
-- opaque ids (gchat `spaces_A_threads_B`) as web. This does the same for the
-- routable id — and it is what unblocks any NEW conversation origin (MCP
-- sessions, behaviour runs) whose id does not happen to match the web packing.
-- Under the old parse such a row was written correctly, passed every ACL check,
-- and was then SILENTLY SKIPPED at render (`if (!threadId) continue`).
--
-- NULL means "this conversation is routed by its conversation_id" — the
-- platform-branch behaviour — so the read collapses to
-- `thread_id ?? conversation_id` with no branch on kind and no skip-on-parse.
ALTER TABLE public.conversations
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS thread_id text;

-- Backfill reproduces the OLD parse EXACTLY so no existing row changes its
-- routable id: only kind='owned' ids carrying the full
-- `{agent_id}_{user_id}_{organization_id}_` prefix yielded a thread id, and only
-- when the remaining suffix was non-empty. Rows that the parse rejected
-- (prefix-only "default thread" ids, foreign-shaped ids) keep thread_id NULL —
-- they were never listed before, and `thread_id ?? conversation_id` must not
-- resurrect them under a different route. The listing keeps skipping them via the
-- same isSafeThreadId/default-thread guards, now applied to a stored value.
UPDATE public.conversations
   SET thread_id = substring(
         conversation_id
         from (length(agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_') + 1)
       )
 WHERE kind = 'owned'
   AND user_id IS NOT NULL
   AND conversation_id LIKE agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_%'
   AND length(conversation_id)
       > length(agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_');

-- migrate:down
-- squawk-ignore ban-drop-column -- rollback path for the column introduced here
ALTER TABLE public.conversations
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS thread_id;

The thread listing derived each row's **routable id** by parsing `conversation_id` at read time:

This is the same defect the `platform` column already fixed — that column exists precisely because deriving the label from the id string mislabelled opaque gchat ids (`spaces_A_threads_B`) as web. Its comment says so: *"Label from the EXPLICIT stored platform, not by parsing the id."*
