Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

This is a technical design memo for one engineer who's mid-decision — utilitarian treatment, not editorial. Let me write it.

**Design plan.** Color: near-black ink `#14161A` on warm-neutral paper `#FAF9F7`; slate-blue accent `#3A5C8C` for structure; muted rust `#A3462F` for the defect path; sage `#4A6B52` for the resolved path; hairline `#D8D5D0`. Type: Georgia for prose (this is an argument to be read), system-ui for labels/UI, ui-monospace for code and ids. Layout: single 68ch column, with the three-generation history as a bordered table and each option as a bordered block carrying a verdict chip — the structure encodes "this bug has recurred," which is the actual thesis.

Design memo · conversations.thread_id

Why the routable-id fix keeps coming back

You called my last change a workaround. You're right — and the reason is that I fixed the third instance of a bug without fixing what generates it.

The pattern

A conversation's identity is a string. Its routable id, its platform, and its origin are all packed into that string, and every reader unpacks them again. Three separate places have independently reimplemented that unpacking:

GenMechanismFate
1 extractThreadIdFromConversationId — fuzzy reverse-parse of the raw string Replaced. Its own successor's docstring calls it a heuristic.
2 webThreadIdFromConversationId — prefix strip from known columns Deleted by this PR. Silently dropped any id it couldn't parse.
3 regexp_match(conversation_id, '_watcher_([0-9]+)_run_') in SQL Still live. Untouched by this PR.

A fourth already exists in spirit: the platform column was added precisely because deriving the label from the id mislabelled gchat's spaces_A_threads_B as web. That fix was correct — and it fixed one field.

What my PR actually did

I moved the generation-2 parse from read time to write time and stored the result. That's genuinely better, but the reviewer found it kept the same failure:

An owned conversation with an opaque id — the MCP-session case this work exists to enable — fails the prefix match, stores null, and is dropped by the reader's if (!threadId) continue. Probe: mcp-session-42 → threadId: null → invisible.

And the second blocker is worse, because it's structural: during a rolling deploy, old replicas keep writing rows with no thread_id while new replicas hide them. My one-time backfill can't cover rows created after it runs.

The patch I started writing — a reader fallback that calls the parse I'd just deleted — is the workaround you sensed. It reinstates generation 2 as a safety net.

The three options, honestly

Conform the MCP id to the web packing

Workaround

Make MCP mint {agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}_mcp-{sessionId} so the existing parser accepts it. Zero read-path changes; ships today.

It works by making one origin impersonate another. The next origin has to learn the trick, and the string keeps carrying meaning no schema declares.

Store thread_id, patch the gaps

Where I am now

The current PR plus an opaque-id branch plus a rolling-deploy fallback. Fixes the instance and leaves the watcher regex untouched.

Two of its three pieces are compensating for the string still being authoritative. That's the tell.

Make the columns authoritative; the id becomes opaque

The real fix

Every origin writes what it knows at creation: platform (already done), thread_id, origin, behavior_id. No reader ever inspects conversation_id — it becomes a pure opaque key. The listing collapses to a projection with no branch on kind and no parse.

This retires all three generations at once, including the watcher regex, and means a new origin needs zero listing changes — which is the actual requirement, since MCP is the origin forcing this and behaviors are next.

How to get there without a risky cutover

The reviewer's own suggestion is the sequencing, and it dissolves the rolling-deploy blocker rather than patching around it:

  1. Add and dual-write. Ship the column and backfill. Writers populate it; readers keep the legacy derivation as fallback. Both replica generations are correct simultaneously — this is the release where the fallback is correct, not a hack.
  2. Drop the fallback. Once no replica can create a null row, readers use the column alone. Now deleting the parse is provably safe rather than hopefully safe.
  3. Migrate the remaining origins. Behaviors write real rows with behavior_id; the regexp_match dies the same way. MCP sessions write theirs with no special-casing at all.

Same code as my current PR — but staged, so the fallback is a declared migration step with an exit condition instead of an unexplained safety net. That's the whole difference between the two.

What I'd do next

  • Reframe PR #2205 as step 1 explicitly: keep the fallback, document its removal condition in the code and the PR body, fix the opaque-id case so MCP works, and add the end-to-end test the reviewer asked for covering packed, default, and opaque ids.
  • File step 2 as a follow-up gated on the deploy, not on someone remembering.
  • Leave the watcher regex alone in this PR — it's the same defect, but it's a separate origin and deserves its own reproduce-and-verify.

You're right, and the code confirms it more strongly than I expected.

Look at what this endpoint is: it caches generated prompts, marks them `stale`, regenerates in the background, and the client **polls every 2.5s while `generating` is true**. That is a Behavior — a standing goal that produces output on a schedule and writes it somewhere readable. It's been reimplemented as a bespoke endpoint with its own cache-staleness protocol and a client-side polling loop.

The redundancy is concrete:

- **Generation on a schedule** → that's what a Behavior does. Cron or interval, no request-triggered regeneration.
- **`stale` + `generating` + 2.5s polling** → a Behavior writes to an entity; the client reads the current value. No staleness protocol, no poll, because there's nothing to wait on — you read whatever the last run produced.
- **The cache** → `entities` already is the cache, with provenance and supersede semantics for free.

And `source: "config" | "agent"` is doing the same job as a Behavior's config-vs-generated distinction.

So the right shape is: a starters Behavior per agent writes prompts onto an entity, and the frontend reads them through the paths that already exist — `search_memory` or the entity read — with zero new endpoints. That also gets you the thing the endpoint can't: the prompts are in the event log, so they're inspectable, correctable, and time-travelable like everything else.

This changes my recommendation on #2208. I said "land the missing `/starters` backend first." That was wrong — it would mean building the redundant thing to satisfy a frontend that shouldn't be calling it. The correct order is the owletto side changing to read from the Behavior output, and *then* the pointer bump. Nothing to build server-side.

I'll note the one thing that would argue against this, so it's a decision and not an assumption: if starters must be generated on-demand for an agent that has never run its Behavior — a brand-new agent's very first chat — then a Behavior on an interval leaves a cold-start gap where the chips are empty. That's solvable (seed at agent creation, or accept empty chips on a new agent), but it's the question worth answering before committing.

I haven't touched anything. #2208 stays unmerged, and its blocker now has a better resolution than the one the reviewer suggested.

That settles the design cleanly. Here's what I found and what I'd build.

## The two halves of owletto#591 are not the same problem

**Suggestion chips (post-turn) — already correct, no duplication.** `POST /internal/suggestions/create` exists, `createSuggestion` exists, and `SuggestionThreadInteraction` replays them on reload. An agent emits suggestions from inside its turn via a worker call. That half of #591 works against a real contract and doesn't need anything.

**Starter chips (fresh draft) — the redundant part.** This is the one that invented `/starters` with `stale`/`generating` and a 2.5s client poll. And it's exactly Behavior-shaped: generate on a schedule, write the result somewhere, let readers read the current value.

So the fix is narrower than "redo #591." Only `useAgentStarters` and its endpoint go.

## The right implementation

A per-agent **starters Behavior** writes its prompts onto the agent's entity. The frontend reads that entity through the paths that already exist — no new endpoint, no `stale`, no `generating`, no polling. `agent-thread.tsx:472-477` only ever touches `data.prompts`, so the consumer barely changes: swap `useAgentStarters` for an entity read and delete the three fields that existed solely to drive the poll.

That also inherits what the endpoint couldn't have: prompts land in the event log, so they're inspectable, correctable via supersede, and time-travelable like all other memory.

## The one thing I want your call on

Cold start. A Behavior on an interval means a brand-new agent has no starters until its first run. Options: seed at agent creation, run the Behavior once on agent create, or accept empty chips on a new agent (the UI already returns `null` when `prompts.length === 0`, so it degrades silently rather than breaking).

Now I can answer properly, and the answer is: **you're largely right, but not entirely.**

## What #2201 actually built

A "hidden starters turn" — it opens a throwaway thread, enqueues an instruction telling the agent to call `suggest_actions` once and finish, then runs it with `source: "starters"` which needs three special-case exemptions: skip the SSE owner-gate, skip the transcript snapshot, and route the result to a per-agent cache.

That's an agent turn dressed as a cache-fill. Three carve-outs in shared code paths exist purely so this turn doesn't look like a turn.

**A Behavior is exactly this, without the carve-outs.** Standing goal, runs headless on a schedule, writes structured output, invisible to chat. `HEADLESS_SOURCES` exists because behaviors already needed headless dispatch. #2201 adds a fourth headless source rather than using the mechanism.

So on the generation half: yes, redundant, and your instinct is right.

## Where you're not right

The **endpoint** isn't redundant. I verified this and it falsified my own earlier claim: the interactions read path is hard-scoped to a `conversationId` built from a `threadId`, and filters `interaction_type = 'approval'`. A fresh draft has no thread, so it genuinely cannot read interactions. Something agent-scoped has to serve prompts to a threadless draft.

The `starter_prompts` column is also fine — config-authored chips served directly, no generation at all. That's the cheap path and it's the right one.

## The honest split

| piece | verdict |
|---|---|
| `starter_prompts` column (config-authored) | keep — no generation, no redundancy |
| `/starters` endpoint | keep — agent-scoped read, no existing path serves it |
| hidden starters turn + 3 source carve-outs | **redundant — this is a Behavior** |
| `stale`/`generating`/2.5s client poll | **redundant — falls out once a Behavior writes it** |

Consolidating means #2201 keeps its column and endpoint, drops `generate-starters.ts` and the `source: "starters"` exemptions, and a starters Behavior fills the store instead. The endpoint becomes a thin read.

That's a substantial change to someone else's 57-file open PR, and it's their call as much as yours — I'd raise it on #2201 rather than rewrite it.

Cheapest immediate unblock, if you want #2202/#2203 landed: merge #2201 as-is, bump #2208, clear drift, then consolidate the generation path as a follow-up. Shipping the carve-outs and removing them later costs less than blocking four PRs on a redesign.

content.text:
Both merged and verified on main. Now your two questions.

## #2203 — what's best long-term

The teammate's (b) is right, and the reason is a design principle worth naming: **`isError` means "the tool failed," not "something went wrong."**

`run_sdk` executes arbitrary caller code. When that code throws, the tool did its job perfectly — it ran the script and returned a faithful report. `SdkScriptResultSchema` encodes this: `success` is required, `error` carries `line`/`column`/`stack`. It's a schema built to express failure *as data*.

The clean rule: a tool with an `outputSchema` reports domain failures through it; `isError` is reserved for the tool itself failing. `query_sql` has no `outputSchema`, so `isError` is its only channel — which is why unknown-table genuinely belongs there. That asymmetry is the whole distinction, and it's stable as you add tools.

Your (a) treated the test as the contract. The tell that it was the wrong layer: after (b), both call sites (a) needed `allowToolError` for pass on the untouched helper. And (a) left `interaction-bridge.ts:1006` prefixing every legitimate script throw with `"Tool error: "` in real agent conversations — a production consequence no test would have caught.

Already merged on your instruction, so this is confirmation rather than a decision.

## #2205 — will option 2 actually kill the debt

Partly. I checked the real scope rather than guessing — there are **two** remaining parse sites, not the sprawl I implied:

- `conversations-store.ts:118` — the prefix strip (my PR already removes this)
- `agent-thread-list.ts:266,272` — the `_watcher_<id>_run_` regex, still live

So "full redesign" means: my current change, plus behaviors writing real rows, plus deleting that regex. That's genuinely the end of the class for conversation ids — the other `startsWith` hits are channel-id and URL-prefix logic, unrelated.

But it doesn't come free. Behaviors writing rows is its own migration with its own backfill and reproduce-verify cycle, and my PR's two blockers still need fixing either way. So option 2 is really option 1 plus a second migration — not an alternative to it.

My recommendation: **option 1 now** (fix the blockers, document the fallback with an explicit removal condition), then behaviors-write-rows as a follow-up that deletes the regex. Same destination, shippable in pieces, and each step is independently verifiable. Doing both at once means one PR carrying two migrations and two backfills — harder to review and riskier to roll back.

The one thing that would change my answer: if you want the regex gone *before* MCP conversations ship, then do them together, because MCP will otherwise be the third origin working around it.

## Where things stand

Merged: **#2202**, **#2203**. Open: **#2205** (blockers unfixed), **#2208** (missing `pi-review`, gated on #2201 which you scoped out).

Confidence: high (98) on the merges — verified both on main by content, not just PR state. High (90) on the #2205 scope, from grepping every parse site. The long-term (b) rationale is design judgment, though it's now consistent across the teammate's analysis and mine.

--                      `{agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}_` prefix
--   kind='platform' -> the whole conversation_id
-- The frontend routes on that `id` (a web thread by threadId, a platform
-- conversation by conversationId), so the parse was reconstructing a field that
-- was simply never stored.
--
-- Parsing the id string is the same defect the `platform` column already fixed:
-- that column exists precisely because deriving the label from the id mislabelled
-- opaque ids (gchat `spaces_A_threads_B`) as web. This does the same for the
-- routable id — and it is what unblocks any NEW conversation origin (MCP
-- sessions, behaviour runs) whose id does not happen to match the web packing.
-- Under the old parse such a row was written correctly, passed every ACL check,
-- and was then SILENTLY SKIPPED at render (`if (!threadId) continue`).
--
-- NULL means "this conversation is routed by its conversation_id" — the
-- platform-branch behaviour — so the read collapses to
-- `thread_id ?? conversation_id` with no branch on kind and no skip-on-parse.
ALTER TABLE public.conversations
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS thread_id text;

-- Derive the routable id for an owned row that did not supply one.
--
-- ROLLING-DEPLOY SAFETY. Prod runs `strategy: RollingUpdate, maxSurge: 1,
-- maxUnavailable: 0` at `replicaCount: 2` (see the summaries-prod overlay), and
-- migrations run as a Helm `pre-upgrade` hook — so this migration commits while
-- BOTH pods still run the OLD writer, and the old pod keeps serving until the
-- roll finishes. Every owned row it inserts in that window has thread_id NULL.
-- A one-time backfill cannot cover them, and a reader-side fallback would just
-- reinstate the read-time parse this migration exists to delete.
--
-- Putting the derivation here fixes that at the only point both writer versions
-- share: the INSERT itself. The old pod's rows get the same thread_id the new
-- pod would have written, so the reader can trust the column unconditionally
-- from the moment the column exists. This is also why it is a trigger rather
-- than a column DEFAULT — a DEFAULT cannot see the row's other values.
--
-- It fires only when thread_id IS NULL, so the new writer (which sends an
-- explicit value, including an explicit NULL for the unroutable default-thread
-- id) is never second-guessed... with one deliberate exception: the
-- default-thread id is exactly the prefix, which yields an empty suffix and is
-- left NULL by the WHERE below. Old and new writers therefore agree on it.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.conversations_fill_thread_id()
RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
  prefix text;
BEGIN
  IF NEW.thread_id IS NOT NULL
     OR NEW.kind <> 'owned'
     OR NEW.user_id IS NULL THEN
    RETURN NEW;
  END IF;

  prefix := NEW.agent_id || '_' || NEW.user_id || '_' || NEW.organization_id || '_';

  IF left(NEW.conversation_id, length(prefix)) = prefix
     AND length(NEW.conversation_id) > length(prefix) THEN
    -- Packed web id: the routable thread id is the suffix.
    NEW.thread_id := substring(NEW.conversation_id from length(prefix) + 1);
  END IF;
  -- Otherwise leave NULL: either the prefix-only "default thread" id (nothing to
  -- route to) or a foreign-shaped id. Both were already unlisted, and
  -- `thread_id ?? conversation_id` must not resurrect them under a new route.

  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER conversations_fill_thread_id
  BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF thread_id ON public.conversations
  FOR EACH ROW
  EXECUTE FUNCTION public.conversations_fill_thread_id();

-- Backfill reproduces the OLD parse EXACTLY so no existing row changes its
-- routable id: only kind='owned' ids carrying the full
-- `{agent_id}_{user_id}_{organization_id}_` prefix yielded a thread id, and only
-- when the remaining suffix was non-empty. Rows that the parse rejected
-- (prefix-only "default thread" ids, foreign-shaped ids) keep thread_id NULL —
-- they were never listed before, and `thread_id ?? conversation_id` must not
-- resurrect them under a different route. The listing keeps skipping them via the
-- same isSafeThreadId/default-thread guards, now applied to a stored value.
--
-- Identical in effect to the trigger above; kept as explicit SQL so the
-- already-committed rows are migrated by a statement that can be reviewed and
-- re-run, not only as a side effect of a future write.
UPDATE public.conversations
   SET thread_id = substring(
         conversation_id
         from (length(agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_') + 1)
       )
 WHERE kind = 'owned'
   AND user_id IS NOT NULL
   AND thread_id IS NULL
   AND conversation_id LIKE agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_%'
   AND length(conversation_id)
       > length(agent_id || '_' || user_id || '_' || organization_id || '_');

fix(server): fill thread_id at the DB boundary for rolling deploys

Migrations run as a Helm pre-upgrade hook while BOTH pods still run the old
writer (prod: RollingUpdate, maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0, replicaCount 2), so
an old replica keeps inserting owned rows with a null thread_id after the
one-time backfill. Reading the column strictly would hide those rows; a
reader-side fallback would reinstate the read-time parse this change exists to
delete.

Fill it in a BEFORE INSERT trigger instead — the one point both writer versions
share. The column is authoritative from the moment it exists, so the reader
needs no fallback and no parse.

Also: match the prefix with left()= rather than LIKE. Underscores in agent/user/
org ids are LIKE wildcards, so 'agQ+usr1+org1+zzz' matched the 'agX_usr1_org1_'
pattern and would have been backfilled with a bogus route.

threadId is now required on ConversationUpsert so a new origin must state its
intent rather than silently defaulting to null.

Verified against a scratch Postgres: old-replica mid-roll insert fills
correctly; default-thread, wildcard-shaped and platform ids stay null; both
upsert variants preserve the stored value; up/down/replay all clean.
EOF

cat > /tmp/prbody.md <<'EOF'
## What

`conversations.thread_id` stores an owned web conversation's route segment, instead of reconstructing it by parsing `conversation_id` on every list read.

The parse was generation 2 of the same defect: its own docstring called the thing it replaced a heuristic. The `platform` column already exists for exactly this reason — deriving a field from the id string mislabelled opaque ids (gchat `spaces_A_threads_B`) as web. This does the same for the routable id.

## Why the trigger (the interesting part)

The first version of this PR was rejected for not being rolling-deploy safe, and my first attempt to fix that added a reader-side fallback — which just reinstated the parse the PR exists to delete.

The premise is real. Prod runs `RollingUpdate, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` at `replicaCount: 2` (`summaries-prod` overlay), and migrations are a Helm `pre-upgrade` hook. So the migration commits while **both** pods still run the old writer, which keeps inserting owned rows with a null `thread_id` after the one-time backfill. A backfill cannot cover them.

The fix belongs at the one point both writer versions share: the INSERT. A `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF thread_id` trigger fills the packed case, so the column is authoritative from the moment it exists — no reader fallback, no parse, no follow-up release needed to remove a temporary shim.

It fires only when `thread_id IS NULL`, so the new writer's explicit value (including an explicit null) is never second-guessed.

## Also fixed

- **`LIKE` → `left()=` in the backfill.** Underscores in agent/user/org ids are `LIKE` wildcards, so `agQ+usr1+org1+zzz` matched the `agX_usr1_org1_` pattern and would have been backfilled with a bogus route. Caught by `make review-fix`; verified real.
- **`threadId` is now required** on `ConversationUpsert` — a new origin must state its intent rather than silently defaulting to null.
- `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS` before `CREATE`, so the embedded migrator can replay.

## Deliberately NOT in scope

Opaque owned ids (an MCP session, a behaviour run) still store null and stay unlisted. Storing them verbatim would list them and then 404, because the read path **re-packs** the id — `readThreadMessages` and the interactions query in `agent-history.ts` both call `buildApiConversationId(threadId)`. Making those origins work means teaching the read path to address a conversation by its stored id, which is a separate change. There's a comment on `threadIdFromApiConversationId` recording this so it isn't rediscovered.

The `regexp_match(conversation_id, '_watcher_([0-9]+)_run_')` in `agent-thread-list.ts` is generation 3 of this defect and is untouched here — separate origin, deserves its own reproduce-and-verify.

## Verification

Migration exercised against a scratch Postgres (schema + real `up`/`down` sections, verbatim):

| case | result |
|---|---|
| old replica inserts mid-roll, no `thread_id` | filled → `thread-MIDROLL` ✅ |
| default-thread (prefix-only) id | stays NULL ✅ |
| wildcard-shaped id `agQ+usr1+org1+zzz` | stays NULL ✅ (was the `LIKE` bug) |
| platform row | stays NULL ✅ |
| upsert 2nd turn, old writer omits `thread_id` | preserved ✅ |
| upsert 2nd turn, new writer sends it | preserved ✅ |
| `down` then re-`up` | clean, `UPDATE 0` on replay ✅ |

Tests: `agent-history-routes.test.ts` 22 pass / 0 fail. The four `threadIdFromApiConversationId` cases were mutation-tested — reverting the behaviour fails 2 of 4.

`make pre-pr` clean (build, typecheck, knip, lint, naming).

**Owed:** the two `conversations-*` integration suites need `DATABASE_URL` with pgvector and did not run locally — CI covers them.
EOF

## What I fixed

**Blocker 2 — rolling-deploy safety.** I checked the deploy mechanics rather than assuming. Prod is `RollingUpdate, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, replicaCount: 2`, and migrations are a Helm `pre-upgrade` hook — so the migration commits while both pods still run the old writer. The blocker was real.

The fix is a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger in the same migration that adds the column. It fills `thread_id` at the one point both writer versions share, so the column is authoritative immediately. No reader fallback, no parse, and no follow-up release needed to remove a shim — which is what made the previous attempt a workaround.

**A real bug in my own SQL.** `make review-fix` caught that the backfill used `LIKE`, where underscores in agent/user/org ids act as wildcards. `agQ+usr1+org1+zzz` matched the `agX_usr1_org1_` pattern and would have been backfilled with a bogus route. Verified against Postgres, now `left()=`.

**Blocker 1 — I was wrong, and the fixer was right.** I'd made opaque ids store verbatim so MCP rows would list. Tracing the read path showed `readThreadMessages` and the interactions query both *re-pack* the id via `buildApiConversationId(threadId)` — so an opaque value would list in the sidebar and then resolve to a conversation id no row has. Listable but unreadable. I kept the fixer's semantics and added a comment recording why, so it isn't rediscovered.

That means **MCP conversations still don't show up** — this PR unblocks it but doesn't deliver it. Making that work needs the read path to address conversations by stored id, which is the follow-up.

## Merged

**#2205** → `7e79027eb` on main. Verified by content, not PR state: trigger live in the migration, zero parse fallbacks in the reader.

CI: 22 pass. `integration` (5m8s) ran the pgvector suites I couldn't run locally — that closed the last real gap in my verification and is why the second review scored higher without a single code change.

## What actually got fixed

The rolling-deploy blocker was real: prod is `RollingUpdate, maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0` at 2 replicas with a Helm `pre-upgrade` migration hook, so the migration commits while both pods still run the old writer. The fix is a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger — the one point both writer versions share — so the column is authoritative immediately, with no reader fallback and no follow-up release to remove a shim. That's the difference from the version you called a workaround.

`make review-fix` also caught a genuine bug in my SQL: `LIKE` treats underscores in agent/user/org ids as wildcards, so `agQ+usr1+org1+zzz` matched the `agX_usr1_org1_` prefix and would have been backfilled with a bogus route. Now `left()=`, verified against Postgres.

## Two things I got wrong, and one still open

I'd made opaque ids store verbatim so MCP rows would list. Tracing the read path showed `readThreadMessages` and the interactions query both *re-pack* the id — an opaque value would list and then 404. The fixer was right; I kept its semantics and left a comment recording why.

**So MCP conversations still don't appear in Recent.** This PR unblocks that work but doesn't deliver it — the read path has to address conversations by stored id first. That's the thing you originally asked about, and it's the natural next PR.

Also still live: the `_watcher_<id>_run_` regex at `agent-thread-list.ts:266` — generation 3 of this same defect, deliberately out of scope.

2. **Read-path change** to make MCP conversations actually listable (the original ask).

## Do workarounds still exist? Mostly no.

**Nothing from #2205 is a workaround.** The reader fallback I'd written was deleted; the trigger is a real fix at the right layer. The only conditional left in that path is `threadId` staying null for opaque ids, which is a *deliberate scope boundary* with a comment explaining it, not a shim.

**The watcher regex is a different thing than I called it.** I've been describing it as "generation 3 of the same defect." Having read it: it isn't. It's an aggregation over `agent_transcript_snapshot` that groups runs by watcher to produce **one sidebar entry per behavior, not per run**. The comment says watcher runs deliberately get no `conversations` row because downstream correlation depends on the raw id shape.

So it's not a parse-instead-of-column workaround — it's a genuine derived rollup with an intentional design reason. Making behaviors write rows means also giving them a per-behavior grouping key, which is real design work, not deletion. I was wrong to lump it in.

That leaves one honest item and one open question:

# Design question: make MCP-client conversations appear in the web sidebar

Repo: /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu (bun workspace, TS, Postgres). Read the real files before answering.

## Goal
A user connects an MCP client (ChatGPT, Claude Desktop) to Lobu and calls tools like
`search_memory`. Those sessions should show up in the web app's conversation sidebar
("Recent") and be openable, the same way Slack threads already do.

## What just shipped (PR #2205, commit 7e79027eb)
`conversations.thread_id` now stores the ROUTABLE id explicitly instead of the reader
re-parsing it out of `conversation_id`. A `BEFORE INSERT` trigger
(`conversations_fill_thread_id`, db/migrations/20260727150000_conversations_thread_id.sql)
fills it for packed web ids, which made it rolling-deploy safe.

Deliberately left out of that PR: opaque owned ids (an MCP session id) still store
`thread_id = NULL` and stay unlisted. See the NOTE on `threadIdFromApiConversationId`
in packages/server/src/gateway/services/api-conversation-id.ts.

## The two facts that define the problem

**1. Nothing writes a conversations row for MCP.**
`upsertConversation` has exactly ONE caller: packages/server/src/gateway/orchestration/
message-consumer.ts:477 — the queue consumer. MCP tool calls never enqueue a message,
so they never produce a row. (Verified by grep; mcp-handler.ts has no reference.)

**2. The read path RE-PACKS the id, so an opaque id can't be read even if a row existed.**
Two sites rebuild the conversation id from parts instead of using a stored value:
  - packages/server/src/gateway/services/agent-thread-list.ts:353 (`readThreadMessages`)
  - packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts:667 (interactions replay)
Both call `buildApiConversationId({agentId, userId, organizationId, threadId})`, which
produces `{agentId}_{userId}_{orgId}_{threadId}`. Feed it an opaque id like
`mcp-session-42` and you get `agent_user_org_mcp-session-42` — a conversation id no row
has. So the thread would list in the sidebar and then render empty.

Note a SECURITY property of the current re-pack: because `userId` is baked into the
constructed id, a user can only ever address their OWN conversations. Any replacement
must preserve that. `getAuthorizedAgentScope` (agent-history.ts:412) supplies an
authenticated `agentId`/`organizationId`/`userId`.

Relevant existing index: `conversations_listing` on
(organization_id, agent_id, last_activity_at DESC) WHERE archived_at IS NULL.
There is no index on thread_id.

## Also relevant
MCP sessions are ~1hr sliding TTL (`SESSION_MAX_AGE_MS`, packages/server/src/mcp-handler.ts:52).
The transcript for a conversation lives in `agent_transcript_snapshot`, addressed by
conversation_id. Behaviors/watchers deliberately get NO conversations row — the sidebar
derives one entry per behavior by aggregating snapshots
(agent-thread-list.ts:259, `regexp_match(conversation_id, '_watcher_([0-9]+)_run_')`).

## What I want from you
The user's words: "what's the best fix ... we can cut the corners and make it work properly."
I read that as: minimum work that is genuinely correct, not a hack that needs undoing later.

Please answer concretely:

1. **Read path.** Which is right, and why?
   (a) Look the row up by (organization_id, agent_id, user_id, thread_id) and use its
       stored `conversation_id`. Kills the re-pack; one code path for packed + opaque.
       Costs an indexed lookup per read and needs a new index.
   (b) Keep the re-pack, fall back to treating threadId as a raw conversation id when
       no transcript exists. No new query on the common path, but two paths and a
       fallback shaped like the one already rejected in #2205.
   (c) Something better.

2. **Write path.** Where should the MCP conversations row be created? The MCP tool
   handler? A shared helper both the queue consumer and MCP call? Something else?
   What should `agent_id` be, given MCP tool calls are not bound to an agent the way a
   chat dispatch is? (Prod orgs all have `system_agent_id = lobu-builder`.)

3. **Is one row per MCP SESSION the right grain**, given the 1hr TTL — or should it be
   per OAuth client, or something else? What actually makes a good sidebar entry?

4. **Scope.** Can this be one PR, or must the write and read sides be split? What is the
   smallest change that is genuinely correct rather than a shim?

5. **What am I missing?** Be adversarial. Point out anything in the above I have wrong.

Be specific and cite file:line. Prefer the simplest correct design over the most general.

Codex is running (first attempt died — it doesn't support `gpt-5.1-codex-max` on this account; retrying on the default model). I'll report its verdict when it lands.

Meanwhile my own investigation turned up something that reframes the question, and I think it matters more than the read-path choice:

## MCP tool calls have no conversation to show

Three findings, each verified:

**No transcript.** `agent_transcript_snapshot` is written only by the worker, via a worker token scoped to a run (`transcript-routes.ts`). An MCP tool call has no worker and no run, so it produces nothing to render.

**No conversations row.** `upsertConversation` has exactly one caller — the queue consumer at `message-consumer.ts:477`. MCP never enqueues.

**But there IS a durable record.** `recordToolInvocationAudit` (`tools/audit.ts:112`) writes a `tool_invocation` event per call, carrying org, `created_by`, `client_id`, and tool name. That's exactly what you described seeing: *"i see the logs in events but don't see the conversation."*

So the sidebar's unit is a conversation with a transcript, and MCP produces a **stream of tool invocations with no messages**. Writing a `conversations` row for an MCP session would create an entry that lists and then opens to nothing — the same listable-but-unreadable failure I hit in #2205, just one layer up.

That means "cut the corners and make it work properly" probably isn't the read-path lookup I was about to build. The real question is what an MCP entry should *show*, and there's a promising answer: `mcp_sessions` already stores `session_id`, `user_id`, `organization_id`, `client_id`, `requested_agent_id`, and `last_accessed_at` — everything a sidebar entry needs, with the tool-invocation events as its content.

That's plausibly a **derived** entry, like behaviors already are, rather than a `conversations` row.

I want codex's independent take before committing to that, since it's a bigger call than the read-path choice and I'd rather not build the wrong thing twice in one session.

Confidence: **95** on the three findings (each grepped and read, not inferred). **60** on "derived entry is the right model" — that's my read, unvalidated, and exactly what I'm asking codex to attack.

I'll come back with its answer and a concrete recommendation.

7	The query should require:
8	
9	```sql
10	organization_id = ?
11	AND agent_id = ?
12	AND user_id = ?
13	AND thread_id = ?
14	AND kind = 'owned'
15	AND archived_at IS NULL
16	```
17	
18	Then `/threads/:threadId/messages` should:
19	
20	- Resolve the row once.
21	- Return 404 if it is absent.
22	- Read messages using the returned `conversation_id`.
23	- Use that same ID for interaction replay.
24	- Never call `buildApiConversationId` on a history read.
25	
26	That removes both current reconstruction sites at [agent-thread-list.ts:353](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/services/agent-thread-list.ts:353) and [agent-history.ts:667](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts:667). `buildApiConversationId` remains useful when creating a new web dispatch, but not for resolving stored history.
27	
28	The owner columns become the security boundary. That is stronger and more explicit than relying on `userId` being embedded inside a string. `getAuthorizedAgentScope` supplies authenticated scope at [agent-history.ts:412](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts:412), and the resolver independently proves that this route belongs to that user.
29	
30	Add a **unique partial index**, not merely a non-unique lookup index:
31	
32	```sql
33	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY conversations_owned_route
34	ON public.conversations (
35	  organization_id,
36	  agent_id,
37	  user_id,
38	  thread_id
39	)
40	WHERE archived_at IS NULL
41	  AND kind = 'owned'
42	  AND user_id IS NOT NULL
43	  AND thread_id IS NOT NULL;
44	```
45	
46	The URL contains no platform discriminator, so two active rows cannot safely share that tuple. A unique index makes the route unambiguous instead of choosing whichever row happens to be newest.
47	
48	Option (b) is the wrong shape: it reintroduces string interpretation, makes absence of a transcript control identity resolution, doubles reads on failures, and can mask broken materialization.
49	
50	## 2. Write path and agent identity
51	
52	Create or refresh the row at the **MCP `tools/call` boundary**, not at initialization and not inside `executeTool`.
53	
54	The right point is the handler beginning at [mcp-handler.ts:279](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-handler.ts:279):
55	
56	- Initialization creates many sessions that never call a tool.
57	- A successful or failed tool attempt is meaningful sidebar activity.
58	- `executeTool` is shared with non-MCP entry points ([execute.ts:1](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/execute.ts:1)); putting conversation lifecycle there would materialize REST and worker calls accidentally.
59	- `upsertConversation` is already the appropriate shared persistence primitive at [conversations-store.ts:66](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/services/conversations-store.ts:66). The queue consumer and MCP handler do not need a shared lifecycle wrapper.
60	
61	Materialize only authenticated sessions with non-null `organizationId` and `userId`. Anonymous public-workspace MCP reads cannot safely become owned sidebar entries.
62	
63	Use:
64	
65	- `kind = 'owned'`
66	- `platform = 'mcp'`
67	- `user_id = authenticated user`
68	- `agent_id = authCtx.agentId` when explicitly and validly bound
69	- otherwise resolve `organization.system_agent_id`
70	
71	Do not hardcode `lobu-builder`; the pointer is nullable and deliberately server-controlled at [20260619130000_org_system_agent_id.sql:17](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/db/migrations/20260619130000_org_system_agent_id.sql:17).
72	
73	Also, do **not** mutate `authCtx.agentId` to the builder merely to obtain a sidebar bucket. That value enters tool execution context at [execute.ts:314](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/execute.ts:314) and can affect filtering and attribution. Keep a separate `conversationAgentId` or `displayAgentId`.
74	
75	For title, use the initialized client name plus first tool, for example:
76	
77	- `ChatGPT · search_memory`
78	- `Claude Desktop · query_sdk`
79	
80	The handler already reads `clientInfo` at [mcp-handler.ts:405](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-handler.ts:405), and OAuth activity already persists it at [clients.ts:51](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/auth/oauth/clients.ts:51).
81	
82	## 3. Grain
83	
84	Use one sidebar row per **Lobu MCP activity session**, not per OAuth client.
85	
86	Per-client is far too coarse: a single ChatGPT or Claude registration can produce many unrelated activity periods and possibly multiple users. OAuth client metadata is appropriate for the title/icon, not conversation identity.
87	
88	However, the MCP transport session is not guaranteed to equal a ChatGPT/Claude chat. MCP defines it as logically related client-server interactions, not as a host conversation, and `tools/call` carries a tool name and arguments but no standardized host thread ID. [MCP transport session management](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports) therefore supports session-level grouping, but not the claim that it reproduces the external chat.
89	
90	So:
91	
92	- Mint a separate `mcpConversationId` at MCP initialization.
93	- Persist its mapping on `mcp_sessions`.
94	- Use one-to-one session → conversation today.
95	- Do not expose or persist the transport session ID as the durable conversation identity.
96	- Let the `conversations` row and transcript survive the one-hour transport expiry.
97	
98	This also avoids coupling product history to the current protocol transport. Lobu is pinned to MCP `2025-03-26` at [constants.ts:28](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/core/src/constants.ts:28), while the draft protocol is already moving away from protocol-level sessions. [MCP draft changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/changelog)
99	
100	A good entry is therefore “ChatGPT MCP activity — search_memory”, not an asserted copy of the ChatGPT conversation.
101	
102	## 4. Scope and rollout
103	
104	This should be **two deployments**, preferably two PRs.
105	
106	PR 1 — read/expand:
107	
108	- Add the unique owned-route index.
109	- Add the row resolver.
110	- Remove both read-side repacks.
111	- Resolve interaction replay using the same stored ID.
112	- Add wrong-user, wrong-org, opaque-ID, archived-row, and duplicate-route tests.
113	- Introduce explicit MCP/read-only routing metadata in the thread DTO.
114	
115	PR 2 — write/materialize:
116	
117	- Mint and persist the MCP conversation key.
118	- Materialize the row on first `tools/call`; refresh activity on later calls.
119	- Record MCP-visible activity.
120	- Add MCP call → sidebar list → open history end-to-end coverage.
121	
122	A single rolling deployment is not fully safe: as soon as a new pod writes an opaque MCP row, an old pod can receive the history request and still re-pack it. A feature flag activated only after every old pod has drained could make one PR safe, but it is more operational machinery than two releases.
123	
124	## 5. What is missing
125	
126	The largest omission is that **there is no MCP transcript**.
127	
128	`agent_transcript_snapshot` is written by workers and requires a real `runs.id`; its schema makes `run_id` non-null at [baseline.sql:425](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/db/migrations/00000000000000_baseline.sql:425), and the worker route verifies run ownership before inserting at [transcript-routes.ts:217](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/gateway/transcript-routes.ts:217). The MCP handler only executes and formats the result at [mcp-handler.ts:285](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-handler.ts:285).
129	
130	Therefore:
131	
132	- Do not invent fake `runs` rows just to force MCP activity into worker snapshots.
133	- Do not write local JSONL; that violates multi-replica correctness.
134	- Add a small append-only durable `mcp_conversation_entries` store, recording tool name, input, returned content/error, timestamp, and call ID.
135	- Have the resolved history reader map those entries into `AgentThreadMessage` objects.
136	- Be honest that Lobu can show the tool-call timeline, not the surrounding host prompts and assistant prose it never received.
137	
138	Other concrete traps:
139	
140	- Owned rows are currently hardcoded to `platform: "web"` at [agent-thread-list.ts:213](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/services/agent-thread-list.ts:213). Without changing this, an MCP entry appears writable and the web composer will dispatch a different packed conversation.
141	- The current non-web route cannot simply be reused: it assumes a channel-shaped platform ID and applies channel visibility at [agent-history.ts:760](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts:760). An opaque MCP ID will 404.
142	- Access to the system agent is currently limited to owner/admin at [agent-history.ts:394](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent-history.ts:394). If ordinary members may use MCP, they will create rows they cannot open. Fix this with row-owned history authorization; do not globally widen `scope=all`, because that scope currently returns every owned conversation at [conversations-store.ts:263](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/gateway/services/conversations-store.ts:263).
143	- The UI needs an explicit `readOnly` or route-kind field. Platform alone should not mean both identity origin and writability.
144	- Record only actual `tools/call` activity, not keepalives, resource reads, or session refreshes.
145	- Expiring/deleting `mcp_sessions` must not archive or delete conversation history.
146	- MCP-originated approval provenance is currently absent because external MCP has no source conversation context. If approval cards must replay, thread the durable MCP conversation ID into approval attribution without pretending MCP is a reply-capable chat transport.
147	
148	So the smallest genuinely correct feature is: **row-owned route resolution + a read-only MCP activity transcript + MCP-bound materialization, rolled out read-first/write-second**. Anything smaller produces either an empty sidebar item, an authorization hole, or a fake “conversation” Lobu cannot actually reconstruct.

I've verified every load-bearing claim. Here's the answer.

## Codex's verdict, and what I verified

It agreed with option **(a)** on the read path, and improved it. But the headline is its answer to question 5, which reframes the whole thing.

**The core finding — no MCP transcript exists, and one can't be faked.** `agent_transcript_snapshot.run_id` is `NOT NULL` (baseline.sql:430), and the write route verifies run ownership. So MCP activity can't be stored there without inventing fake `runs` rows — which it says explicitly not to do, and I agree. This matches what I'd found independently and what you saw: events exist, conversations don't.

Its conclusion, which I think is right: **a `conversations` row alone produces a sidebar entry that opens to nothing.** That's the listable-but-unreadable failure from #2205, one layer up. So the honest minimum is bigger than the read-path lookup I was about to build.

**Four traps it caught that I had missed or got wrong:**

1. **`platform: "web"` is hardcoded** at `agent-thread-list.ts:213` for every owned row. An MCP entry would render as writable, and the composer would dispatch to a *different* packed conversation. Verified.

2. **Authorization hole.** `canUseSystemAgent` requires `m.role IN ('owner','admin')` (agent-history.ts:394). An ordinary member using MCP creates rows they cannot open. Verified — this is real and I'd have hit it.

3. **`system_agent_id` is nullable**, server-controlled, no FK. My "all 7 prod orgs have lobu-builder" was a snapshot, not an invariant. Don't hardcode it. Verified in the migration comment.

4. **Don't mutate `authCtx.agentId`** to get a sidebar bucket — it flows into tool execution and affects filtering/attribution. Use a separate display field.

**Where it went further than needed:** it wants a unique partial index on `(org, agent, user, thread_id)` rather than a plain one. That's a good call — the URL has no platform discriminator, so two active rows sharing that tuple would make routing ambiguous.

**Where I'd push back:** it proposes a new `mcp_conversation_entries` table. Tool invocations are *already* durably recorded as `tool_invocation` events (`tools/audit.ts:112`) with org, user, client, and tool name. Before adding a table I'd check whether those events can back the reader — that's the difference between a two-PR feature and a three-PR one.

## What I recommend

Codex says two PRs, read-first then write. I agree on the split, with the sequencing rationale being the one that convinced me: a single rolling deploy isn't safe, because a new pod could write an opaque row while an old pod still re-packs it on read — the same overlap window that shaped #2205.

So: **PR 1 = read path** (row-owned resolution, unique index, kill both re-packs, `readOnly`/route-kind in the DTO). Genuinely correct on its own, no behavior change until rows exist. **PR 2 = write path + activity reader**, once we've settled whether audit events suffice.

I've stopped before building, because this is materially larger than what I described last message and the scope call is yours. Two things worth your input:

- **Is a tool-call timeline actually the product you want?** Lobu never receives the host's prompts or the assistant's prose — only tool calls. An honest entry reads "ChatGPT · search_memory", not a reproduction of the ChatGPT conversation.
- **Should I check the audit-events route first?** If those events can back the reader, PR 2 stays small and no new table is needed.

Confidence: **95** on the four traps and the no-transcript finding (each grepped and read against main). **85** on two-PR sequencing. **50** on whether audit events suffice — genuinely unknown until I look.

That's the full picture. Your instinct is right, and it's a significantly better design than either proposal.

## Your approach wins, and it's much smaller

**Why it's better, not just cheaper.** Codex and I were both trying to make MCP activity *look* like a conversation. It isn't one — Lobu only ever sees tool calls, never the host's prompts or the assistant's prose. Every design that renders it as a thread has to invent something: a fake transcript, a new entries table, a `readOnly` flag to stop the composer dispatching into it. Your version tells the truth: it's activity, so link to the activity view.

It also deletes most of codex's trap list. No hardcoded `platform: "web"` problem, because it's not a thread entry. No composer-dispatch hazard. No `mcp_conversation_entries` table. No fake `runs` rows.

**What already exists** (verified, not assumed):

- Audit events are written per tool call — `semanticType: 'audit'`, with `organizationId`, `createdBy` (user), `clientId`, and tool name (`tools/audit.ts:112`)
- The events surface has a **URL-backed filter system** with `semanticTypes`, `agentId`, `platforms`, `runIds` and a deep-link/merge layer (`events-tab/navigation.ts`, `lib/event-filters.ts`)

So "link to events with the right filter" is largely wiring filters that already exist.

**The one real gap:** `client_id` is **not** a filter today. That's what distinguishes "ChatGPT's activity" from "all audit events." Adding it is a narrow, well-precedented change — it follows the exact shape of `agentId`, which already filters on a metadata field.

## On the 10-second refresh

Worth a caveat: polling every 10s on a page backed by the `events` table means a repeated query per open tab. Before fixing an interval I'd check what the events list query costs — the repo has a standing lesson about verifying the query plan before perf work. A slower default (~30s) with refresh-on-focus is usually indistinguishable to a user and much cheaper. Easy to tune once measured.

## What I'd build

1. Add `clientId` to the event filter set (server + URL param), mirroring `agentId`
2. Surface MCP activity as an entry that deep-links to events filtered by `semanticType=audit` + `clientId`
3. Live-refresh on that view, interval chosen after measuring the query

That's plausibly **one PR**, not the two-then-three codex scoped — and it needs no schema change, since the data is already there.

content.text:
You asked me to interview you, so I'll leave the questions standing rather than answer them for you and start building. Here they are in plain text, with my recommendation on each.

## The three decisions

**1. Entry model — how far to generalize now**

The sidebar already has your pattern: `behavior` entries list in Recent but route to the behavior's page (`app-sidebar.tsx:545`), driven by `platform` + a typed id (`behaviorId`). MCP wants exactly that shape, pointing at filtered events instead.

- **(a)** Follow the behavior precedent exactly — `platform: "mcp"` + a `clientId` field, one more branch. Smallest diff, perfectly consistent. The if-chain grows to 4 cases.
- **(b)** Server returns a typed route descriptor (`route: {kind, params}`), sidebar renders any entry without switching on platform. The connectors page reuses the same descriptor later.
- **(c)** Ship the plain branch now, generalize when the connectors page actually lands.

**My recommendation: (a), leaning (c).** You said "design it in a good way" for the connectors page, and I'd normally jump to (b) — but the connectors page doesn't exist yet, and designing its contract from one imagined consumer is how you get an abstraction that fits neither. The behavior precedent is *already* the generalization; MCP is its second user. When the connectors page arrives you'll have two real consumers and the right shape will be obvious.

**2. Entry grain — what is one row?**

- **One per connected client** ("ChatGPT", "Claude Desktop") — one stable row each, latest activity time.
- **One per MCP session** — a new row per reconnect.

**My recommendation: per client, fairly strongly.** Sessions have a 1hr sliding TTL, so a single ChatGPT install would litter Recent with near-identical rows that expire. Per-client maps 1:1 to `events.client_id` — a real indexed column with an FK to `oauth_clients` — survives session expiry, and reads naturally on a connectors page later, exactly like a feed does.

**3. Refresh**

You said ~10s. I'd want to measure the filtered events query first — the repo has a standing lesson about verifying the query plan before perf work, and a repeated full-filter query per open tab is that shape. My guess is 15–30s plus refresh-on-focus is indistinguishable to you and much cheaper, but that's a guess until measured.

## What I'm confident about regardless of your answers

No schema change. `events.client_id` is already a real indexed column (`idx_events_client_id`), audit events already carry `client_id` + `created_by` + org per tool call (`tools/audit.ts:112`), and the events filter system is already URL-backed. The only genuinely new backend capability is **adding `clientId` to the events filter** — and it's simpler than the existing `agentId` filter, which reaches into `metadata->>'agent_id'` while ours is a plain indexed column.

Also worth restating plainly, since it was your original question: **there's no dead code to remove here.** #2205 already deleted both parsing generations and left no leftovers. The watcher regex turned out to be a designed rollup, not debt — I was wrong to call it that. And the read-path re-pack stays correct for packed web threads, because your design routes MCP away from conversations entirely. That's the real win: your approach makes the thing I was about to surgically remove unnecessary to touch.

Answer the three and I'll build it. If you'd rather I just pick, say so and I'll go with (a)/per-client/measure-first.

input.sql: SELECT e.client_id, oc.client_name, oc.user_id AS oc_user, count(*) AS event_count, max(e.created_at) AS last_at FROM events e LEFT JOIN oauth_clients oc ON oc.id = e.client_id WHERE e.semantic_type = 'audit' AND e.client_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1,2,3

content.text:
Excellent — real data confirms the design works. ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Lobu CLI all present with `client_name` populated, and audit events carrying `client_id`.

But it also surfaces two design problems I need to solve before coding:

**1. Same client registers repeatedly** — "Lobu CLI" appears 6 times with different `client_id`s. Per-client-id grain would show 6 "Lobu CLI" rows.
**2. Two rows have no `oauth_clients` join** (null name) — orphaned client_ids.

Let me check how bad the duplication is.

input.sql: SELECT coalesce(oc.client_name,'(unregistered)') AS client_name, count(DISTINCT e.client_id) AS distinct_client_ids, count(*) AS events, max(e.created_at) AS last_at FROM events e LEFT JOIN oauth_clients oc ON oc.id = e.client_id WHERE e.semantic_type='audit' AND e.client_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1

content.text:
This is exactly why I checked real data first. Grouping by `client_id` gives 13 sidebar rows for 6 actual clients — "Lobu CLI" alone would appear 6 times. Grouping by `client_name` gives the 6 you'd actually want.

That's a real design correction, and it changes the filter I'm about to build. Let me verify the fix before committing to it.

input.sql: SELECT oc.client_name, count(DISTINCT oc.id) AS registrations, count(DISTINCT oc.user_id) AS distinct_users, count(DISTINCT oc.organization_id) AS distinct_orgs FROM oauth_clients oc GROUP BY 1

content.text:
Confirmed and it's clean: every `client_name` maps to exactly **1 user and 1 org**. So grouping by `client_name` is safe — it can't merge two different users' activity into one row, which was my security concern.

Let me report where this stands, since it's a natural checkpoint and there's an important finding.

## Backend done and proven

Committed as `b2093a0ee`. The `client_id` filter works end-to-end against real Postgres.

**Evidence, not assertions:**
- 5/5 new tests, covering both the list path and the search path

**Two things the work uncovered that changed the design:**

**1. Grouping by `client_id` would have been wrong.** I queried prod before coding, and "Lobu CLI" has **6 distinct client_ids** — a client gets a new `oauth_clients` row every time it re-registers. Per-client-id grain would put 6 identical "Lobu CLI" rows in your sidebar. Grouping by `client_name` gives the 6 real clients you'd expect (ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Lobu CLI, Owletto for Mac, unregistered). I also verified the safety property: every `client_name` maps to exactly **1 user and 1 org**, so name-grouping can't merge two people's activity. That's why the filter takes an **array**.

**2. The tool schema was a required second step.** My first test run failed — `getContent` validates against the generated `read_knowledge` schema, so adding the internal type wasn't enough. Exactly the kind of gap a typecheck hides and a real run catches.

I also found `agent_id` was filtered at **four** sites, not two — including classification stats. I wired all four, because a stats distribution computed over a wider set than the rows it labels is just wrong.

The frontend half: the sidebar entry grouped by `client_name`, the deep link into events filtered by those client ids + `semantic_type=audit`, and the refresh interval.

I was ready to argue for a typed route descriptor — server tells the client where each entry goes, client stops switching on `platform`. It's the same principle that made #2205 right: **the reader shouldn't re-derive what the writer already knows.**

But the evidence doesn't support building it now:

- **The DTO drift is real but small.** `behaviorId?` is the only kind-specific field so far. Adding `clientIds?` makes two. That's a smell, not yet a defect.
- **The repo's own rule** says deleting or restructuring needs structural evidence, not anticipation.

So the honest long-term answer is: **follow the behavior precedent now, and let the connectors page be the forcing function for the abstraction** — with two real consumers, the right shape is derivable instead of guessed. There's one thing I'd do differently for the long term, though, and it's worth doing now because it's cheap and it's where the actual leverage is:

**Group by `client_name` server-side, in `listAgentThreads`.** Not client-side. That's the piece the connectors page will want verbatim — "one row per connected client, with its ids" is the same query for both surfaces. content.text:
That's conclusive.

## No — MCP clients don't write to `conversations`

I verified it three ways rather than repeat my earlier claim:

- **Only two writers exist** for that table: `upsertConversation` (queue consumer) and `resolvePinnedSelection` (sandbox pin). I'd previously missed the second one — it turns out to be the agent-run pin path, called only from `message-consumer.ts` and `deployment-manager.ts`.
- **The MCP path imports neither.** `mcp-handler.ts`, `execute.ts`, and `audit.ts` have zero references to either writer.
- **What MCP writes instead** is `recordToolInvocationAudit` — an audit event per tool call (`execute.ts:262`).

Both conversation writers require a **run**. An MCP tool call has no run — no worker, no queue message, no transcript. That's the structural reason, not an oversight someone forgot to wire up.

## So why did I raise a separate endpoint?

Not because of the write side — because of **scoping**. `listAgentThreads(organizationId, agentId, userId)` is agent-scoped, and it's the sidebar's only source. MCP activity is user-and-org scoped: a tool call isn't bound to an agent at all.

So an MCP entry has no natural agent to belong to. That's the tension, and it's independent of which table anything writes to.

**But your instinct points at something better than either option I gave you.** If we made MCP write a `conversations` row, everything else falls out for free — the sidebar already lists that table, the entry gets an agent scope, and no new endpoint is needed.

The catch is what codex flagged and I confirmed: a `conversations` row without a transcript produces a sidebar entry that **opens to nothing**. That's the listable-but-unreadable failure from #2205 all over again.

Except — and this is the part that changes with your events-page idea — **that failure only matters if the entry opens a transcript.** If the MCP entry deep-links to the filtered events page instead, an empty transcript is irrelevant. It never reads one.

So the design that actually holds together is: **MCP writes a `conversations` row** (`kind: 'owned'`, `platform: 'mcp'`, agent = the org's system agent, `thread_id` = null since it isn't thread-routable), and the sidebar routes `platform: 'mcp'` to the events page rather than the transcript — exactly like `platform: 'behavior'` routes to the behavior page today.

That is genuinely better than my separate-endpoint suggestion: one listing source, no new endpoint, no new grouping query, and the connectors page later reads the same table.

One consequence worth naming: a `conversations` row is per-`(org, agent, platform, conversation_id)`, so the grain becomes whatever `conversation_id` we mint. To get your "one row per client" it should be the client id — which reintroduces the 6-ids-per-`client_name` problem I found in prod. Two options: mint per client-name, or accept per-registration rows.

Want me to go with the `conversations`-row design? I think you're right and it's the better long-term shape — I'd just want to settle the grain question before writing it.

## What

Connected MCP clients (ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, the CLI) now appear in the Recent sidebar. Clicking one opens the events timeline filtered to that client's tool activity.

## Why this shape

An MCP tool call writes **no `conversations` row** — both writers of that table (`upsertConversation`, `resolvePinnedSelection`) require a run, and an MCP call has no run, no worker, and therefore no transcript. So a conversation row would list an entry that opens to nothing.

What MCP *does* write is an audit event per tool call (`recordToolInvocationAudit`), carrying `client_id`, `created_by` and org. That's the record that exists, so the entry points at it. Same pattern as `behavior` entries: listed in Recent, derived from the trail, opens elsewhere.

No new table, no migration, no fake transcript, no new endpoint.

## Grouped by client_name, not client_id

A client mints a **new** `oauth_clients` row every time it re-registers. Prod has **6 ids for "Lobu CLI"** — keying on the id would repeat one client six times down the sidebar.

Grouping by name is safe because the query pins `oc.user_id` and `oc.organization_id`: two users' activity can never merge into one row. Verified in prod — every `client_name` maps to exactly 1 user and 1 org.

That's also why `clientIds` is a **list** everywhere: DTO, URL param, and API arg.

## Verified against prod

The exact listing query, run against production data:

| client_name | registrations collapsed |
|---|---|
| Claude | 1 |
| Lobu CLI | **6 → one entry** |
| ChatGPT | 1 |
| Codex | 1 |
| Owletto for Mac | 2 |

5 clean rows, which is the sidebar this is meant to produce.

## The subtle bit: positional SQL slots

`client_id` took slot **$12** in the shared search WHERE template, which shifts `orgScope` and every downstream index (exclude, visibility, entity-types, cursor) to **$13**. That class of mistake typechecks perfectly and fails only against a real Postgres — often as wrong rows rather than an error.

So the integration test exercises **both** query paths and was **mutation-tested**: reverting the shift fails 2 of 5 tests.

`client_id` is threaded through all four sites that already filter `agent_id` — list, search, include-superseded, and classification-stats — so a stats distribution can't be computed over a wider set than the rows it labels.

## Test evidence

| new `client_id` integration tests | 5/5 |
| new event-filter round-trip tests | 3/3 |
| server vitest (334 files) | **2860 pass**, 0 fail |
| owletto vitest (106 files) | **920 pass**, 0 fail |
| agent-history bun tests | 22/22 |
| `make pre-pr` | clean |

All server tests ran against real Postgres with pgvector.

## Not in scope

Live refresh on the events view. I wanted to measure the filtered query's cost before picking an interval rather than guessing at 10s — the data is already fresh on navigation.

content.text:
You were right to ask, and the answer is: I didn't, and I shouldn't have opened the PR without it.

## What skipping E2E cost

Rather than boot it, I claimed 80% confidence from typechecks and unit tests. Then `make review` found **2 real blockers** — both runtime failures that every one of my 3,780 passing tests missed:

1. **`clientIds` was a string, not an array.** With `fetch_types: false` the driver returns `'{a,b}'` for a bare `array_agg`, so the sidebar's `.join()` would have **thrown on render**. This repo already has a helper written for exactly this trap. The feature would have been visibly broken the moment you clicked it.

2. **One duplicate row per agent.** The sidebar fans out `listAgentThreads` *per agent* and concatenates. My query ignored `agentId`, so every agent returned the same MCP rows. They also leaked into `scope=user`, where an `mcp_*` id isn't resumable at all.

Both fixed, both **mutation-tested** — reverting `to_jsonb` fails the 2 shape assertions, reverting the scope gate fails the scope test. 2864 server tests, 920 owletto tests green.

## And a third thing E2E-hunting caught

While rebasing I found the codesmith bot had repointed the submodule to owletto **main**, which doesn't contain my sidebar commit. My entire frontend half was silently absent from the PR diff. Fixed by merging main into the feature branch (merge, not rebase — the submodule rule) and repointing.

That's the "stale pointer silently drops merged work" trap, and I'd have shipped straight into it.

## Honest status

**Still not E2E'd.** I tried: stood up Postgres, ran migrations, booted the dev server three times. It kept dying — first because `setsid` doesn't exist on macOS, then because the vitest harness reset the schema under it and it failed the schema-version check. I stopped rather than burn more time on process babysitting.

So what I have is strong integration-level proof against real Postgres — including the exact runtime shape that was broken — but **not a browser click**.

Confidence: **88** on the backend (prod-verified query, mutation-tested, full suites green). **70** on the rendered UI — the specific bug that would have broken it is now fixed and asserted, but I still haven't seen the row.

The remaining E2E is worth doing before merge, and it needs a clean boot: separate DB from the test harness, server started detached properly. I'd rather do that than merge on 70.
