E2E is done. Here's what was actually blocking it.

## The issue

Not process management — that was my misdiagnosis last message. The real cause: **the server refuses to boot without a populated `schema_migrations` ledger**, and the vitest harness applies all 183 migrations *without writing one*. So every boot died at `readAppliedSchemaVersion` with `relation "public.schema_migrations" does not exist`.

Fix: create the ledger and record the 183 migrations the harness had already applied. Server came up in 20 seconds.

I also wasted two attempts on `setsid` (doesn't exist on macOS) and on assuming the server self-migrates for external Postgres (it doesn't). Both were me guessing instead of reading the error.

## E2E result — live server, real Postgres, seeded to match prod shape

```
--- MCP ENTRIES ---
{"title":"ChatGPT",  "clientIds":["mcp_e2e_chatgpt"],
 "clientIdsIsArray":true, "joined":"mcp_e2e_chatgpt"}
{"title":"Lobu CLI", "clientIds":["mcp_e2e_cli_a","mcp_e2e_cli_b"],
 "clientIdsIsArray":true, "joined":"mcp_e2e_cli_a,mcp_e2e_cli_b"}
--- scope=user ---
mcp rows in scope=user: 0
```

All three things the review flagged are now proven fixed against a running system:

- **2 rows, not 3** — "Lobu CLI" collapsed its two registrations into one entry
- **`.join()` works** — `clientIdsIsArray: true`. This is the bug that would have thrown on render; unit tests passed while it was broken
- **`scope=user` is empty** — no per-agent duplicates, no unresumable `mcp_*` ids in the chat list

One thing E2E surfaced that I then checked: the entry id is `mcp_Lobu CLI` — it contains a space. Harmless, because it's only a React `key`; the link navigates via `search` params, not a path segment. Worth knowing rather than assuming.

## State

**PR #2211** — 21 pass, 1 fail, 1 pending. The fail is `check-drift`, the same unmerged-owletto-commits check you admin-merged past on #2203; it's red because my owletto branch isn't on main yet, which is expected for a paired PR.

Also caught during this round: the codesmith bot had repointed the submodule to owletto main, silently dropping my entire frontend commit from the diff. Fixed by merging main into the feature branch and repointing.

Confidence: **93** — backend query verified against prod data, both blockers mutation-tested, full suites green (2864 server + 920 owletto), and now the actual runtime shape confirmed through a live server. Not 100 because I verified the data layer end-to-end, not a browser screenshot of the rendered row.

Ready to merge when you want, or I can re-run `make review` first since the last verdict was on the pre-fix commit.

Now I have the full picture, and it changes my answer to your first question.

## Where connected apps are listed today

**`GET /api/{org}/clients`** already exists and is purpose-built for exactly this. It returns MCP clients *plus* messaging clients, with `status: connected|disconnected`, `authState`, `lastSeenAt`, `assignedAgentId`, `capabilities`, `userAgent`, `firstParty`, and a revoke endpoint (`DELETE /mcp/:clientId`).

There's a typed client hook (`useConnectedClients`) — but it's consumed in exactly **one** place: a behavior-builder panel. **There is no connected-apps page.** The data and API exist; the surface doesn't.

## So: workaround or solution?

Honestly — **the events filter is a solution; the sidebar entry is a workaround.**

The filter (`client_id` on events) is genuinely right. It's a real indexed column, it fills a real gap, and `read_knowledge` can now answer "what did ChatGPT do here." That stands on its own regardless of what happens to the UI.

The sidebar entry is weaker than I presented it, for a reason I only see now that I've found `client-routes.ts`: **I derived a second, poorer notion of "connected client" from audit events, when a richer one already existed.** Mine knows a name and a timestamp. The existing one knows connection status, auth state, assigned agent, capabilities, and can revoke. Two sources for the same concept is the duplication you keep telling me to avoid.

It also puts a *connected app* in a list called **Recent**, next to conversations. That's a category error — an app isn't a conversation, and the only reason I put it there is that you asked for it in Recent before either of us knew the clients API existed.

## What I'd do

The connectors page you mentioned isn't a "later" nice-to-have — it's where this belongs, and the backend for it is **already built**. `GET /api/{org}/clients` needs a page, not a new endpoint.

Concretely:

1. **Keep** the `client_id` events filter (`b2093a0ee`) — independently correct, no dependency on any of this.
2. **Build the connected-apps surface on `useConnectedClients`**, which gives you status/revoke/last-seen that my derived entry can't.
3. **Drop or defer the sidebar entry** — or, if you still want Recent to show MCP activity, source it from the clients API rather than a parallel audit-event query.

I should have grepped for an existing clients API before deriving my own. That's the same mistake as earlier in this session: building before checking what's there.

Two ways to go, and it's your call: **split the PR** (land the filter now, redo the surface on the clients API), or **repoint the sidebar entry** at `useConnectedClients` within this PR. I'd take the split — the filter is ready and the surface deserves to be designed against the API that already models it.

input.content:
# Design question: is MCP activity a CONVERSATION with an external origin?

Repo: /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu (bun workspace, TS, Postgres). Read the real files.

## The user's framing (this is the question to evaluate)

"I thought one conversation can be mapped to internal and external, meaning it's
living somewhere else like Slack, and Recent automatically shows it?"

They are pointing out that the `conversations` model ALREADY expresses "this
conversation lives somewhere else":

  packages/server/src/gateway/services/conversations-store.ts:28 classifyConversation()
    platform 'api'  -> { kind: 'owned',    storedPlatform: 'web' }
    anything else   -> { kind: 'platform', storedPlatform: <platform> }

Slack is not special-cased anywhere. A Slack message flows:
  inbound -> message-consumer.ts:465 classifyConversation -> upsertConversation
  -> conversations row (kind='platform', platform='slack')
  -> listAgentThreads (agent-thread-list.ts) lists it in Recent
  -> the UI opens it READ-ONLY by raw conversation_id
     (app-sidebar.tsx: `if (!isWeb)` -> /conversations/$conversationId)

So the user's question is: why is MCP not simply another `platform` value?

## What I built (and now doubt)

PR #2211. I DERIVED sidebar entries for MCP clients by aggregating audit events:

  agent-thread-list.ts — a query grouping `events` (semantic_type='audit') joined
  to oauth_clients by client_name, emitting platform:'mcp' entries carrying
  clientIds[], which deep-link to the events timeline filtered by those ids.

Plus a genuinely separate, self-standing change: a `client_id` filter on the
events/get_content query paths (events.client_id is a real indexed column,
idx_events_client_id, FK -> oauth_clients, written per tool call by
recordToolInvocationAudit in tools/audit.ts:112).

## What I found AFTER building it (the reason I'm asking)

There is ALREADY a purpose-built connected-clients API I did not know about:

  packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts:197  GET /api/{org}/clients
    returns MCP clients + messaging clients with:
      status: connected|disconnected, authState, lastSeenAt, assignedAgentId,
      capabilities, userAgent, firstParty, externalUrl, linkedUserName/Email
  packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts:302  DELETE /mcp/:clientId (revoke)
  owletto: src/lib/api/clients.ts — typed `useConnectedClients` hook already exists,
  but is consumed in exactly ONE place (a behavior-builder panel). There is NO
  connected-apps page.

So my derived "MCP client" notion is a SECOND, POORER model of a concept the
codebase already models better.

## The hard constraint

An MCP tool call has NO transcript. `agent_transcript_snapshot.run_id` is NOT NULL
(baseline.sql:430) and the write route verifies run ownership
(gateway/transcript-routes.ts). MCP calls have no run and no worker. So a
conversations row for MCP would list an entry that opens to NOTHING — unlike Slack,
whose rows DO have transcripts written by the worker that processed the message.

Also relevant: `upsertConversation` has exactly one caller (message-consumer.ts:477,
the queue consumer) and `resolvePinnedSelection` (sandbox-store.ts:266) is the only
other writer. Neither is reachable from the MCP tool path (mcp-handler.ts /
tools/execute.ts import neither).

MCP sessions have a 1hr sliding TTL (mcp-handler.ts:52) but oauth_clients rows are
long-lived. A client RE-REGISTERS under the same client_name: prod has 6 distinct
client_ids for "Lobu CLI". Every client_name maps to exactly 1 user and 1 org.

## Questions

1. **Is the user right?** Should MCP be a `platform` value on `conversations`
   (kind='platform', platform='mcp') so Recent lists it with zero new mechanism —
   the same way Slack does? What breaks, given there is no transcript to open?

2. If yes, what is the unit of an MCP "conversation" — the MCP session (1hr TTL),
   the oauth client registration, or something else? What would its
   `conversation_id` be, and who writes the row?

3. If no — if MCP activity is genuinely NOT a conversation — then is the right
   surface the EXISTING `GET /api/{org}/clients` (which already models connection
   status and revoke), with a connected-apps page? And should the sidebar entry be
   dropped entirely, or sourced from that API instead of my derived audit query?

4. **Is my derived audit-event aggregation a workaround?** Be blunt. I am asking
   because I built it before finding client-routes.ts.

5. Should the `client_id` events filter be kept regardless? It is independently
   useful ("what did ChatGPT do here") and has no dependency on the UI decision.

6. What am I missing? Be adversarial and cite file:line.

Prefer the simplest design that does NOT create a second model of an existing
concept. Say plainly if the answer is "delete what you built and use the existing API".

Codex is running. Here's what I've established while waiting — and your framing turns out to be **right about the model but decisive against my implementation**.

## You're right: the model already does this

`conversations` already expresses "lives somewhere else," and Slack isn't special-cased:

```
classifyConversation(platform):
  'api'         → kind: 'owned',    platform: 'web'
  anything else → kind: 'platform', platform: <platform>
```

A Slack message flows: inbound → consumer classifies → `upsertConversation` → row → Recent lists it → opens read-only by raw id. Zero Slack-specific code. So "why isn't MCP just another platform value?" is exactly the right question.

## Why MCP can't ride that path

Three things I verified, and the third is decisive:

**No transcript.** `agent_transcript_snapshot.run_id` is `NOT NULL`, written only by a worker holding a run-scoped token. Slack rows *have* transcripts because a worker processed the message. MCP has no run and no worker — so a `conversations` row would list an entry that opens to nothing.

**No conversation id.** The MCP tool path has **zero** references to `conversationId`. Not an unwired gap — the concept isn't there.

**It isn't conversation-shaped.** Prod data, all MCP audit activity:

| client | tool | calls |
|---|---|---|
| Lobu CLI | run_sdk | 4,823 |
| Lobu CLI | query_sql | 1,235 |
| Claude | run_sdk | 848 |
| ChatGPT | run_sdk | 314 |

Two tools, thousands of calls. That's an API client's call log, not a thread. "Lobu CLI · 4,823 run_sdk calls" isn't something you open like a Slack conversation.

The asymmetry: Slack is a place where *messages* live. MCP is a *credential* making tool calls. Both are "external," but only one is a conversation.

## So, workaround or solution?

**The sidebar entry is a workaround** — and worse than I realized when you asked. I derived a second, poorer model of "connected client" from audit events, when `GET /api/{org}/clients` already models it properly with status, auth state, last-seen, assigned agent, capabilities, and revoke. Two models of one concept is exactly the duplication you've told me repeatedly to avoid. I built it before grepping for what existed.

**The `client_id` events filter is a solution.** Real indexed column, real gap, independently useful, no dependency on any UI decision.

## Where connected apps should live

The connectors page — and its backend is **already built**. `useConnectedClients` exists and is consumed in exactly one place (a behavior-builder panel). There's no page. That's the actual missing piece, and it's a UI-only build against an existing API.

Still thinking. Let me answer your question directly with what I can verify — the analogy is close but breaks in one specific place.

**Connection ≈ yes. Feed ≈ no.**

An `oauth_clients` row already *is* connection-shaped: stored credential, a status (`active_token_count > 0` → connected/disconnected), an `authState`, revocable via `DELETE /mcp/:clientId`. It's a connection that happens to live in a different table because it arrived through OAuth registration rather than the connector flow.

But a **feed** is a *scheduled pull*: `schedule`, `next_run_at`, `checkpoint`, `last_sync_at`, `items_collected`, plus repair machinery. Lobu decides when to fetch and tracks where it left off.

MCP is the inverse — the client pushes calls whenever it wants. There's no schedule to set, no checkpoint to resume from, nothing to sync. Modeling it as a feed would leave most of that table meaningless and imply controls (pause, run-now, backfill) that don't exist.

So the accurate mapping is:

| concept | MCP equivalent | exists? |
|---|---|---|
| connection | `oauth_clients` row | **yes** — with status + revoke |
| feed (scheduled pull) | — | **no** — MCP is push-driven |
| the events it produced | `events` + `client_id` | **yes** — my filter |

What sits "under the connection" isn't a feed. It's **the activity that connection produced** — which is exactly the `client_id`-filtered events timeline, the one piece of my PR that's genuinely right.

That gives a clean structure, and it matches how you described connectors:

**Connected apps page** → one row per client (from the existing `GET /api/{org}/clients`, which already has status/last-seen/revoke) → click through to **its activity**, the events filtered by `client_id`. Same shape as opening a connection and seeing what it did.

description: MCP client activity is a CONNECTION (oauth_clients), not a conversation or feed — surface via existing /api/{org}/clients, not derived audit rows

Decided 2026-07-27 after building the wrong thing twice and having codex refute it.

**The model.** An MCP client is **connection-shaped**, not conversation-shaped and
not feed-shaped:
- `oauth_clients` row already = credential + status + revoke → a connection.
- NOT a feed: `feeds` is a scheduled PULL (`schedule`, `next_run_at`, `checkpoint`,
  `items_collected`). MCP is push-driven; those columns would be meaningless.
- NOT a conversation: the MCP tool path has ZERO `conversationId` references, and
  `agent_transcript_snapshot.run_id` is NOT NULL (worker-only), so there is no
  transcript to open.

**The surface already exists and had no page:** `GET /api/{org}/clients`
(`packages/server/src/lobu/client-routes.ts:197`) returns MCP + messaging clients
with status/authState/lastSeenAt/assignedAgentId/capabilities, plus
`DELETE /mcp/:clientId` to revoke. `useConnectedClients` (owletto
`src/lib/api/clients.ts`) is typed and consumed in exactly ONE place (a
behavior-builder panel). Build the Connected Apps page on THIS, with "view
activity" drilling into events filtered by `client_id`.

**Why the derived-audit approach was wrong** (deleted, do not retry):
- `recordToolInvocationAudit` → `buildPayload` only instruments **`run_sdk` and
  `query_sql`**; every other tool returns null and writes NOTHING
  (`tools/audit.ts` ~line 56-101). So audit events are a PARTIAL log, never
  "everything a client did".
- Deriving a client inventory from events is wrong in both directions: a client
  with no qualifying event disappears; a REVOKED client with old events persists.
- `client_name` is not a stable identity (prod: 6 client_ids for "Lobu CLI", 18
  registrations → 6 names). Group only in the clients API with explicit canonical
  identity + explicit multi-registration revoke semantics.

**Recent sidebar caveat.** Recent IS a union (behaviors are listed with no
`conversations` row), so "not a conversation" alone does not disqualify an entry.
But `useRecentAgentThreads` fans out `scope:"all"` **once per agent** and
concatenates with no cross-agent dedup — so any ORG-GLOBAL row emitted from the
agent-scoped `listAgentThreads` duplicates once per agent. Behaviors are safe
because they are genuinely agent-scoped. Verified by reproduction: 2 agents →
`["mcp_Lobu CLI","mcp_Lobu CLI"]`.

---
name: reference_get_content_score_path_drops_filters
description: get_content sort_by=score + entity_id builds its OWN filter object that silently drops agent_id/client_ids — a filter added to the other paths does NOT apply there
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`packages/server/src/tools/get_content/handler.ts` has FOUR filter application
sites, not one. Adding a filter to the obvious ones still leaves a silent hole.

The trap: the `sort_by === 'score' && entityId` branch (~line 377) constructs a
**separate** `filters` object for `getNormalizedScoreContent` / `…Count`. It
enumerates fields explicitly, so anything not listed is silently dropped — the
query returns UNFILTERED rows rather than erroring.

Confirmed missing there as of 2026-07-27: `agent_id` (pre-existing) and
`client_ids`. So this is a CLASS, not a one-off.

When adding an events/get_content filter, wire ALL of:
1. `utils/content-search/types.ts` — the option type
2. `utils/content-search/params.ts` — shared positional param + WHERE skeleton
3. `utils/content-search/list-path.ts` — appended condition (params.length-indexed)
4. `utils/content-search/search-path.ts` — FIXED positional slot
5. `tools/get_content/query.ts` — `fetchIncludeSuperseded` AND
   `fetchClassificationStats` (stats scope must match list scope or the
   distribution is computed over a wider set than the rows it labels)
6. `tools/get_content/schema.ts` — the PUBLIC tool schema; `getContent` validates
   against it and rejects unknown args, so an internal-type-only change fails at
   runtime with "Invalid arguments for read_knowledge"
7. **the score path above**

**Positional-slot hazard:** `params.ts` and `search-path.ts` are positional
MIRRORS. A new slot (`$12`) shifts every downstream index — `buildOrgScopeWhere`
`baseParamIndex`, `excludeParamIdx`, visibility, entity-types, cursor. A mismatch
TYPECHECKS FINE and fails only against real Postgres, often as wrong rows rather
than an error. Always add an integration test that exercises BOTH the list path
and the search path, and mutation-test it by reverting the shift.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.conversations_fill_thread_id()
RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $
DECLARE prefix text;
BEGIN
  IF NEW.thread_id IS NOT NULL OR NEW.kind <> 'owned' OR NEW.user_id IS NULL THEN
    RETURN NEW;
  END IF;
  prefix := NEW.agent_id || '_' || NEW.user_id || '_' || NEW.organization_id || '_';
  IF left(NEW.conversation_id, length(prefix)) = prefix
     AND length(NEW.conversation_id) > length(prefix) THEN
    NEW.thread_id := substring(NEW.conversation_id from length(prefix) + 1);
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END; $;
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS conversations_fill_thread_id ON public.conversations;
CREATE TRIGGER conversations_fill_thread_id
  BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF thread_id ON public.conversations
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION public.conversations_fill_thread_id();
```

cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'BODY'
## What

Adds a `client_ids` filter to `read_knowledge` / the events query paths, and fixes a class of silently-dropped filters on the score-sort path.

**1. `client_ids` filter (new capability).** `events.client_id` is a real indexed column (`idx_events_client_id`, FK → `oauth_clients`) written per tool call, but nothing could filter on it. Now you can ask "what did this MCP client do here". Accepts an array because a client that re-registers gets a new `oauth_clients` row under the same name (prod: "Lobu CLI" has 6 ids).

**2. Dropped-filter class on the score path (bug fix).** `get_content` has four filter-application sites. The `sort_by === 'score' && entity_id` branch runs through its own builder (`buildFilterConditionsAndJoins`), and both it and the handler's filters object enumerate fields explicitly — so anything not listed is **silently dropped**. The query returns unfiltered rows rather than erroring, which is the worst failure shape: you ask for one client and get everything, led by whatever scored highest.

Three filters were missing there, so this is a class, not an instance:

| filter | status |
|---|---|
| `client_ids` | added with the filter itself |
| `agent_id` | pre-existing hole |
| `analyzed_by_behavior_id` | pre-existing hole — the handler *always* forwarded it; the builder had no clause |

Fixed all three in one pass per the "fix the class, not the instance" rule.

## Red → green evidence

New test file failing against the unfixed source — the filter is dropped and the highest-scoring non-matching row leads:

```
× client_ids scopes score-sorted rows to that client
  AssertionError: expected [ 'chatgpt high score row', …(2) ] to deeply equal [ 'cli low score row' ]
× agent_id scopes score-sorted rows to that agent
× total count matches the filtered rows, not the unfiltered set
  AssertionError: expected [ { id: 1, …(43) }, …(2) ] to have a length of 1 but got 3

 Tests  3 failed | 1 passed (4)
```

After the fix, whole events integration suite:

```
 Test Files  32 passed (32)
      Tests  149 passed (149)
```

## Mutation testing

Each predicate was individually neutered (`TRUE OR <predicate>`) to prove the tests bite and are correctly isolated:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `agent_id` → no-op | 1 failed — only the `agent_id` test |
| `client_id` → no-op | 2 failed — the `client_ids` test + the count test |
| `analyzed_by` → no-op | 1 failed — only the `analyzed_by_behavior_id` test |

The count assertion exists because rows and `total` come from two separate queries sharing one builder; fixing only the row query would leave pagination lying.

Fixtures deliberately give the **non-matching** rows the higher score, so a dropped filter surfaces them first and fails loudly rather than passing by accident on ordering.

## Notes for review

- The `client_id` filter took positional slot `$12` in the search path, shifting `orgScope`/`exclude`/`visibility`/`entity-types`/`cursor` to `$13`. That kind of drift typechecks fine and fails only against real Postgres, so both the list path and the search path are exercised against a real DB.
- `review-fix` also suggested two classification-filter tests. Dropped: verified against unmodified `origin/main` that the fixture they introduce fails there identically, so they assert a **pre-existing** gap unrelated to this branch. Worth a separate look, not this PR.
- Scope note: this branch previously carried a derived "connected MCP clients in the Recent sidebar" feature. That was removed — `GET /api/{org}/clients` already models connected clients better (status, authState, lastSeenAt, revoke), and a second derived model was the wrong shape. The surface for it will reuse that existing API instead. Only the events filter, which stands on its own, remains here.

## Testing

- [x] `make pre-pr` — build, strict typecheck, knip, biome, exposed-surface naming
- [x] Events integration suite: 149/149 against Postgres 18 + pgvector
- [x] Red → green captured for every fixed filter
- [x] Mutation-tested each predicate individually
BODY

content.text:
## Answering your question

**Is it premature optimization? Mostly yes — but one part of your instinct is right and worth keeping.**

**"Should an MCP client show as a connector too?"** — No, and the schema says why. `connections.connector_key` is `NOT NULL`, and there is **no MCP connector definition** anywhere in `packages/connectors/`. More telling: `connections` and `oauth_clients` have **zero foreign keys between them, in either direction**. They aren't two views of one thing that drifted apart — they were never linked. A connector is something *you* configure to reach *out* to a third party (credentials, a connector key, an auth profile). An MCP client is something that registers itself to reach *in*. Making one look like the other means inventing a fake `connector_key` and a fake connection row per registration, and then keeping them in sync forever. That's the "second model of an existing concept" trap I already fell into once on this branch.

**"Group under the feed for all conversations?"** — This is the part that doesn't fit. `feeds` is a **scheduled pull**: it has `schedule`, `next_run_at`, `checkpoint`, `items_collected`. MCP is push-driven — the client calls us, on its own cadence, with no schedule to store and no checkpoint to advance. Those five columns would all sit NULL forever. And there's no conversation to group: the MCP tool path has no `conversationId`, and `agent_transcript_snapshot.run_id` is `NOT NULL` and worker-only, so there's no transcript to open.

**What I think you're actually reaching for, and it's real:** the *unifying* idea — "one place to see everything attached to this workspace" — is sound. But the unification belongs at the **page level**, not the schema level. `infrastructure/` already holds devices, models, sandboxes, deployments; clients become a fifth item there. Same shelf, same visual treatment, no forced table marriage. That's what you told me earlier when you pushed back on over-consolidating surfaces: similar structures aren't the same page.

So: **premature to merge the tables; not premature to want them on one screen.** The screen is PR 2, and it doesn't need any schema change to happen.

Let me check the review.

cat > /tmp/pr2214.md <<'BODY'
## What

Closes #2214.

The classification branch of `listContentInternal` scoped org-wide listings with its own predicate:

```sql
f.entity_ids && ARRAY(SELECT id FROM entities WHERE organization_id = $N)::bigint[]
```

Every other listing path — including the non-classification branch of the *same file* (`list-path.ts:447`) — uses `buildOrgScopeWhere`, a three-way OR:

```sql
f.organization_id = $N  OR  EXISTS(entity in org)  OR  c.organization_id = $N
```

The narrow version dropped two whole classes of row:

- **Events with NULL/empty `entity_ids`** (audit rows, system events). Because `&&` against NULL yields **NULL, not false**, these were dropped without ever being evaluated.
- **Events reachable only through their connection's organization.**

Net effect: an org-scoped event with no entity link was invisible to `classification_filters` while remaining visible to every other filter.

## Red → green

Before — asking for a classification returns only the entity-linked row, silently missing the direct-org and connection-bridge rows:

```
× applies classification filters across every organization-scope path
  → expected [ 2 ] to deeply equal [ 1, 2, 3 ]
```

After:

```
 Test Files  33 passed (33)
      Tests  151 passed (151)   # events integration dir
```

The mutation above *is* the regression test: reverting just the org-scope predicate reproduces the original bug exactly, and the assertion names which rows go missing.

## Test coverage

The new integration test pins all three org-scope paths plus the negative cases:

| row | reaches the org via | expected |
|---|---|---|
| direct org row | `f.organization_id` | included (was **dropped**) |
| entity bridge row | entity in org | included |
| connection bridge row | connection's org | included (was **dropped**) |
| foreign row | another org entirely | excluded |
| unclassified row | direct org, no classification | excluded |

There was previously **no end-to-end integration coverage of `classification_filters` at all** — the only references were unit tests asserting it is *rejected* in the `include_superseded` path. That gap is why this survived.

## Second-order find

Switching to the shared builder surfaced a latent coupling. With no entity, `buildThreadMetaCteSql` falls back to binding `$1::bigint`; in this branch `$1` is now the org id (text), so the query failed with `22P02 invalid input syntax for type bigint`. The org branch now passes an explicit always-true entity-link fragment — which is what the existing comment above it already said the org path wanted ("org-wide listings already constrain candidates upstream").

## Testing

- [x] Red → green captured, and the red is reproducible by reverting one predicate
- [x] Events integration: **151/151**
- [x] Full server vitest suite: **2877 passed, 0 failed**
- [x] `make pre-pr` — build, strict typecheck, knip, biome, exposed-surface naming
- [x] `make review-fix` applied; it strengthened the test to cover all three scope paths + foreign-org exclusion
BODY

**RESOLVED 2026-07-27 (both, decided from the code, not preference):**
1. **Authz.** `mcpAuth` only resolves identity — it does NOT authorize a role

2. **Multi-registration.** Revoke operates on ONE `client_id`, so "revoke

   the linked user so one person's Revoke can't disconnect another's client.

`/$owner/memory` with a permissive `pruneSearch`. A "view this client's
activity" deep link needs the memory scope-bar filter wiring; deliberately left

## What

Adds a **Connected Apps** tab under Connect, listing the MCP clients attached to the workspace — and closes two authorization/correctness gaps that building the page exposed.

The API (`GET /api/{org}/clients`) already existed with status, authState, lastSeenAt, capabilities, and revoke. It had **no page** and exactly one consumer (a behavior-builder panel). This adds the page on the existing rails rather than a second model.

## The two decisions, resolved from the code

**1. Authorization — revoke is now owner/admin.**

`mcpAuth` only resolves identity; it authenticates, it does not authorize a role (`auth/middleware.ts` is a one-line delegate to `resolveAuth`). So any org member could revoke a client another member registered, killing that person's live tokens and MCP sessions.

Revoke is now gated on owner/admin, matching `resolveToolAccessLevel`'s elevated tier. **Listing stays open to members** — it exposes no secrets, and hiding it would defeat the point of a page whose job is noticing a rogue client.

> ⚠️ **Behavior change:** member-role callers now get `403` from `DELETE /api/{org}/clients/mcp/:clientId`. This broke a real pre-existing test whose fixture user joins as a plain `member` — which is the gate proving it bites. That test's subject is org *scoping*, not authz, so it elevates its own role rather than asserting the old permissive behavior.

**2. Multi-registration — "revoke ChatGPT" now means ChatGPT.**

A client that re-registers gets a NEW `oauth_clients` row under the same name. Prod has **6 ids for "Lobu CLI"**. Revoking one id left the same app connected through its siblings, so the user disconnects ChatGPT and ChatGPT stays online.

`?scope=all` fans out across the same `(client_name, resolved owner)`. Default stays single-id, so existing callers are unchanged. The UI always sends `scope=all` because its row represents the *app*.

Crucially, the UI's grouping key is the **server's** `registrationGroupKey`, built from the same pair the fan-out matches on — so what a row collapses is exactly what Revoke disconnects. Deriving it client-side risked the two drifting.

## Two bugs found along the way

**Ownerless clients could join someone else's revoke group.** The first fan-out used `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, so `NULL` matched `NULL` — a legacy registration with no owner would be swept in. It now requires a real `client_name` and owner, resolving a legacy row's owner from its token in this org.

**Cross-replica revocation didn't stick.** `handleMcp` reused an in-memory session without re-checking the persisted row, so a live transport on another pod kept working after a revoke and re-upserted the row the revoking pod had deleted. The persisted row is the cross-replica signal; a missing row now 404s and drops the local session.

## Verification

Every predicate was mutation-tested — the code was broken deliberately to confirm the test fails, and that it fails on the *right* assertion:

| mutation | caught by |
|---|---|
| admin gate → always allow | the 2 authz tests only |
| `scope=all` → always single-id | the fan-out test only |
| owner resolution → back to `NULL`-matches-`NULL` | the fan-out test |
| cross-replica check → disabled | the session-recovery test only |
| group key → ignore the user | "does not merge across different people" |
| `connected` → last-one-wins | (initially **survived** — the test asserted only one ordering; fixed to assert both) |

There's no "view this client's activity" deep link. There is **no `/$owner/events` route** — events live under `/$owner/memory` behind the scope-bar filter wiring. Rather than ship a broken link, that's left for a follow-up now that the `client_id` events filter (#2211) exists to back it.

**Confirmed and it's worse than described.** Listing uses `MAX(ot.user_id)` (lexicographic) while revoke uses newest-token — so on a shared registration the page can display Alice's name while Revoke hits Bob. `MAX(u.name)` and `MAX(u.email)` are independent too, so the name/email pair can be a chimera of two people.

          MAX(u.email) AS user_email,

input.new_string:
INNER JOIN LATERAL (
        SELECT
          -- Owner identity must come from ONE token, picked the SAME way the
          -- revoke path picks it (newest token for this client in this org).
          -- Independent MAX() aggregates would let a shared registration
          -- display one person's name, another's email, and revoke a third —
          -- so the row you click would not be the grant you kill.
          owner.user_name,
          owner.user_email,
          owner.token_user_id,
          COUNT(*) FILTER (
            WHERE ot.revoked_at IS NULL AND ot.expires_at > NOW()
          )::int AS active_token_count
        FROM oauth_tokens ot
        LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
          SELECT u2.name AS user_name, u2.email AS user_email, ot2.user_id AS token_user_id
          FROM oauth_tokens ot2
          LEFT JOIN "user" u2 ON u2.id = ot2.user_id
          WHERE ot2.client_id = oc.id
            AND ot2.organization_id = ${organizationId}
          ORDER BY ot2.created_at DESC, ot2.id DESC
          LIMIT 1
        ) owner ON true
        WHERE ot.client_id = oc.id
          AND ot.organization_id = ${organizationId}
        GROUP BY owner.user_name, owner.user_email, owner.token_user_id

Good news first: this isn't a pending decision anymore — **#2219 is already merged** (`2e505295e` on main, pi-review green), and the follow-up program landed too (#2233 audit stamping, #2239 the org-level session activity endpoint, owletto side included). The page also moved in the final shape: it lives at **Connectors → Apps** (`src/app/$owner/connectors/apps.tsx`), not under infrastructure.

So the real question is "should we now *remove* the Apps page since Recent covers it?" My answer as a teammate: **no — they answer different questions, and only one of them can revoke.**

- The Recent section's "clients" filter (which I just re-read in `home-attention-timeline.tsx`) renders **MCP sessions** from the #2239 endpoint — it's activity. It answers "who talked to us lately."
- The Apps tab renders **standing access** — every registration with a live token — and holds the only Revoke affordance. It answers "who *can* connect right now, and disconnect this one."

The gap between the two is exactly the case that matters for a security surface: an app holding a live token that hasn't opened a session in weeks shows **nothing** in Recent, but it still has full access to the org. Cmd+K searches conversations and entities, not OAuth grants — there's no path from search to "kill this app's access."

Two more practical reasons not to rip it out:

1. Revoke is the hard-won part — owner-scoped, admin-gated, grouped by the server's `registrationGroupKey` so what you see is exactly what `?scope=all` revokes. That took five review rounds to get correct. Deleting the page strands `useRevokeMcpClient` and the DELETE route with zero consumers — the same smell in reverse as the "one-consumer hook means the page is missing" rule.
2. Cost of keeping is near zero: one tab, tests in place, no polling burden beyond what's already shipped.

If your instinct is "two MCP surfaces is one too many," the honest framing is: Recent/clients = the feed (what happened), Apps = the inventory (who has keys). Folding the inventory into the activity feed is the overconsolidation trap we've explicitly rejected before — similar-looking lists doing different jobs.

**Recommendation: keep it as merged, do nothing.** Confidence: high on the merged state and code layout (verified against `origin/main` in both repos just now); medium on "Recent can't substitute" only in the sense that I reasoned from the code paths rather than clicking both pages in prod.

Next actions you could pick from:
- Prod-verify the merged surface once (Apps tab + one revoke round-trip) — that verify is still owed per the program notes.
- If the Apps tab feels buried, a link from the Recent clients filter header ("Manage connected apps →") is a 5-line bridge, not a merge.
- Nothing — close the thread.
should we merge properly or no

No — don't merge the surfaces. Recommendation stands, and here's the concrete reasoning:

**They have incompatible contracts.** The Recent clients filter is a *feed*: recency-bounded, member-visible, answers "what happened." The Apps tab is an *inventory*: must be complete (every live grant, even idle ones), admin-gated, carries a destructive action. If you fold the inventory into the feed you either break the feed's shape (a timeline that also has permanent rows and Revoke buttons) or break the inventory's guarantee (completeness silently bounded by the feed's window). This is exactly the "similar-looking lists ≠ same page" trap we've hit and rejected twice before — separate the goal (one mental place for MCP clients) from the implementation (one component).

**The authz split alone forces two renderings.** Members can see activity; only owners/admins can revoke. A merged page ends up conditionally morphing between two different things, which is more code and more review surface than the two simple pages we have — both of which are already shipped, tested, and green.

**What "merging properly" would actually cost:** redesigning the timeline component to host non-temporal rows, re-plumbing the admin gate into the home surface, re-running the revoke test matrix against a new entry point — all to save one tab. That's negative ROI on a surface that took five review rounds to make safe.

If the itch is discoverability, do the cheap bridge instead: a "Manage connected apps →" link on the Recent clients filter header pointing at Connectors → Apps. One small owletto PR, no server changes, no contract changes. I can do that now if you want it — otherwise the right move is genuinely nothing.
i mean consolidate

The consolidation you're asking about already happened — that was the final shape of the program. The Apps tab sits **under Connectors**, next to connections, so there's one place in the nav where "things that talk to this org" live. That was the page-level unification we settled on.

The remaining question is whether to go one level deeper — make each MCP client an actual connector/connection row — and that's the version I'd still say no to, for the reasons we established with schema evidence before the merge:

- `oauth_clients` and `connections` have no FK in either direction, and there's no MCP connector definition to hang one on. You'd be inventing a synthetic connector type whose `feeds`/config columns are permanently NULL — a schema shim to make two different lifecycles look alike.
- The lifecycles genuinely differ: a connection is something you *install and configure* (credentials flow org→out), an MCP client is something that *registered itself and was granted access* (tokens flow in). "Disconnect" and "revoke" are different operations with different blast radii — we spent five review rounds getting revoke's ownership semantics right precisely because it doesn't behave like a connection delete.
- Everything downstream (audit stamping via session id in #2233, the activity endpoint in #2239, owner-scoped revoke) is keyed on `oauth_clients`/`mcp_sessions`. Rebasing that onto `connections` is a migration with no user-visible payoff — the user already sees one consolidated Connectors area.

So: **consolidated at the nav/page level — done, shipped. Consolidating at the schema level — evaluated, rejected, and I'd hold that line.** The one cheap addition that serves the "one mental place" goal is the bridge link from the Recent clients filter to Connectors → Apps. content.text:
Mystery solved — and it's working as designed, not a bug. Here's what your ChatGPT connection actually does:

**ChatGPT has written 629 events, but zero of them are conversations.** The breakdown: 455 are tool-invocation audit records (the #2233 stamping — every `search_sdk`/`query_sdk` call it makes, with redacted args and its MCP session id), ~170 are config-change records from when it created/edited entity types, feeds, and behaviors, and just 2 are actual content (1 observation, 1 todo — times it deliberately called a save tool).

**Why: MCP is a pull protocol.** When ChatGPT is "connected," it holds OAuth tokens (92 live ones in your org) and calls tools to *read* your memory on demand — it was doing exactly that today at 13:54. It never pushes its chat transcript to Lobu; there's no mechanism in MCP for that. A conversation only lands in Lobu if the client explicitly calls something like `save_memory` mid-chat.

**Why the memory page shows none of this:** `/buremba/memory` browses *content* — entities and events grouped by connections and feeds (`useConnectionConnectorGroups`). ChatGPT's events have no feed, no entities, and `semantic_type` of `audit`/`change`, so they're invisible to that view by design — surfacing 455 "search_sdk completed" audit rows as memories would be noise. ChatGPT activity lives on the two surfaces built for it: **Recent → clients filter** (sessions) and **Connectors → Apps** (the inventory + revoke).

So the split is: Memory = what the org knows; Apps/Recent = who's been reading it. ChatGPT is currently almost pure reader.

If what you actually want is ChatGPT's conversations *becoming* memory, the lever is on the ChatGPT side: its connector instructions need to tell it to call `save_memory` (or an equivalent write tool) when something durable comes up — the 1 observation proves the path works when it bothers. Options from here:

- Strengthen the MCP server instructions so clients proactively save takeaways (that's a prompt change, cheap).
- Accept the current split and do nothing — read-mostly clients are the normal case.
- If you want audit visibility inside memory, that's a deliberate design change we should scope, not a quick toggle.

Found the exact gap — and yes, the redirect is precisely the missing piece. Here's the map:

**Server side: no gap, already done.** The events read path (`read_knowledge`/`get_content`) accepts `client_ids` in its schema, the handler forwards it on every branch (that's what we fixed in #2211), and the SQL filters on the indexed `f.client_id` column. You can filter events by MCP client end-to-end today via the API.

**Frontend side: two small gaps, both in owletto:**

1. **`EventFilters` has no client dimension.** `src/lib/event-filters.ts` supports `agentId`, `watcherId`, `connectionIds`, `feedIds`, `runIds` — each with a URL param and an API mapping (`params.agent_id = filters.agentId` at line 479). There is no `clientId` twin: no `?client=` URL param is parsed, and nothing maps to the server's `client_ids`. So even manually typing a URL can't scope the events page to ChatGPT.
2. **No row links.** The Apps tab rows and the Recent → clients session rows show the client but link nowhere. The bridge you described — click ChatGPT → `/buremba/memory?view=events&client=mcp_client_8hOPs…` — doesn't exist because of gap 1.

The fix is small and mechanical, mirroring the existing `agentId` filter exactly: add `clientId` to `EventFilters` (parse `?client=`, emit `client_ids` in `convertFiltersToApiParams`, show it in the drill-filter banner), then make each client row an `href` into the events view with that param. Roughly 30–50 lines plus tests, owletto-only, zero server changes.

One expectation to set before you click that link: what you'll see for ChatGPT is its **audit trail** — rows like "search_sdk completed" and the config changes it made — because that's all it writes. It's genuinely useful ("what has this app been touching"), but it won't look like conversations, since ChatGPT never sends its chat content over MCP.

Say the word and I'll ship the owletto PR (filter + row links). Alternatives if you'd rather scope differently: link only from the Apps tab (smallest), or also surface the same link from the Recent clients filter rows.

content.text:
"Apps tab" was my sloppy name — in the merged shape it's the **Connected apps** page at `app.lobu.ai/buremba/connectors/apps`. It's the inventory page that #2219 shipped: one row per app that has OAuth access to your org — for you that's ChatGPT, Claude, Lobu CLI, Codex, Owletto for Mac — each showing who it's linked to, last activity, connected status, and an admin-only **Revoke** that kills that app's tokens and live MCP sessions.

You reach it two ways in the current UI:

1. The sidebar dropdown menu → **"Connected apps"** (it sits right under "My devices").
2. Clicking any row in the home Recent → **clients** filter (each session row links to it).

It's not literally a tab in the Connectors tab bar — it's its own routed page hanging off the connectors section, linked from those two places. That's also why you may not have stumbled into it: it's one level deep in a dropdown.

So the redirect idea from before, stated concretely: rows on that Connected apps page (and the session rows in Recent) would deep-link to `/buremba/memory?view=events&client=<id>`, showing that app's event trail — once the ~40-line `clientId` filter gap in owletto's `event-filters.ts` is filled. Want me to ship that?

it can be mcp no? we can have an static connector called mcp clients and we can show the connections feeds under there? and the recent can also redirect the user to the events. if the user clicks the icon they can do the feed of that session

Yes — and this is the first version of the connector idea that actually maps onto existing machinery instead of fighting it. What changed since I argued against it: the schema objection was "MCP clients have no connection row, so consolidating means NULL-riddled fakery." Your proposal inverts that — *give* them real connection rows under a static `mcp` connector, and then every existing surface lights up for free instead of us building a parallel client-filter dimension:

- **Memory page**: groups by `useConnectionConnectorGroups` → "MCP clients" appears as a connector group with ChatGPT/Claude/CLI under it, automatically. This is exactly what you expected to see at `/buremba/memory` and didn't.
- **Events page**: already filters by `connection_ids` and `feed_ids` → the Recent redirect and the click-through need **zero new filter code**, just links.
- **Session drill**: events already carry `mcp_session_id` in metadata (#2233), so "the feed of that session" is a virtual feed reading events by session id — the virtual-feed machinery exists.

The build is server-side, in three pieces:

1. **Static connector definition** `mcp` (built-in, no install flow) + auto-provision a connection row when a client is granted tokens.
2. **Write-path stamping**: MCP-written events get `connection_id` set (today ChatGPT's rows have it NULL — verified in your prod dump) + a one-time backfill from `client_id`.
3. **Lifecycle wiring**: revoke ↔ connection disconnect become the same operation, and the Apps page rows become those connections.

One real design decision before I'd start, and it's the one that took five review rounds last time: **connection granularity**.

- **Per client-group** (one "ChatGPT" connection): cleaner list, but re-opens the shared-registration ownership mess — one connection row, multiple users' grants under it.
- **Per grant** — one connection per (client, user): my recommendation. It matches how connections already work (single owner, private visibility — same as `oauth_account`), makes revoke = disconnect with no ambiguity, and the display problem we fought is dissolved rather than patched. The list shows "ChatGPT — Emre" and "ChatGPT — teammate" as separate rows, which is arguably *more* honest.

Expectation-setting still applies: ChatGPT's feed will be its audit/config trail, not chat transcripts — MCP doesn't push conversations. The connector framing doesn't change that; it just gives the trail a proper home.

Effort: roughly two PRs — server (definition, provisioning, stamping, backfill migration, revoke↔disconnect) then a small owletto pass (retire the standalone Connected apps page into the connector's detail, add the Recent→events links). The 40-line `clientId` filter becomes unnecessary — skip it.

If per-grant granularity sounds right to you, I'll set up the worktree and start on the server PR.
oh actually it makes more sense to put it under agent no?

Honestly — yes, agent framing fits the *thing itself* better than connector framing, and here's the test: a connector's job is bringing data in (Slack, Gmail — you browse their feeds). An MCP client is an **actor** — it opens sessions, reads memory, calls tools, changes config. ChatGPT's trail in your org is "what did this actor do," not "what data did this source sync." That's an agent-shaped question. It also finally resolves the "external agents — UNRESOLVED" placement question left over from the connect-surface merge.

And there's more existing plumbing on this side than I gave credit for:

- Events already have an `agentId` filter wired end-to-end, including the **memory sidebar rail** ("memory written by this agent"). The agent dimension is a first-class filter today; the client dimension isn't.
- Sessions map naturally onto the agents surface's conversation/thread idiom — "ChatGPT's sessions" reads like an agent's conversation list, which is literally what you asked for ("click the icon → feed of that session").
- MCP already has an agent-binding seam (`x-lobu-agent-id`): a client can attribute its work to an agent now. Unbound clients are the invisible ones.

One trap to avoid, though — and it's a rule we established before: **agent binding is attribution, not authorization.** If we create real `agent` rows for ChatGPT, the UI starts implying guardrails, models, and skills govern it. They don't — nothing enforces anything on an external client. Synthetic agent rows would be the same NULL-columns fakery as synthetic connections, plus a safety-misleading UI on top.

So the shape I'd build:

1. **Agents page grows an "External agents" section** — client groups from the existing clients API, visually distinct from internal agents (no model/guardrail affordances, an "unmanaged" badge or similar).
2. **External agent detail page**: sessions (the #2239 endpoint already serves this), activity (events by `client_id`), and access/revoke — the Connected apps page's content moves here and the standalone page retires.
3. **Events/memory get the `client` filter** (the ~40-line owletto gap; server's `client_ids` is already done) so detail links and Recent rows deep-link into the events view. External clients appear in the memory rail alongside agents.

No schema changes, no synthetic rows, no backfill — it's a UI union plus one filter dimension, maybe two small PRs, and it's strictly less work than the connector version.

If you're good with this shape, I'll set up the worktree and start with the filter + links PR (it's the foundation either way), then the agents-surface move.

content.text:
Now I can answer from the actual routing, and the short version is: your instinct is right, and the codebase is already halfway there.

What exists today: `/memory` is an umbrella doing two unrelated jobs behind a `?view=` param — **Context** (entity browse, the default) and **Activity** (the events log). The sidebar's "Activity" row already points at `/memory?view=events`, and `/$owner/activity` already exists *as a route* — it's just a redirect back into `/memory`. The Feeds tab was already amputated from this page earlier. So `/memory` isn't a designed bundle; it's what's left of an older three-tab page. "Why /memory page" has no strong answer anymore.

The split I'd do:

- **`/activity` becomes a real page** (flip the existing redirect): the full events log with the filter bar. Sidebar "Activity" points there. This is also where all the client/agent deep-links from Recent land.
- **Home stays the curated layer, not the firehose.** Home's Recent timeline is collapsed and attention-ranked; the activity log is dense and filter-heavy. Making the raw log the home would crowd the chat surface. Instead: Recent keeps its filters and gets "See all →" into `/activity`. If you later decide home *should* be the log, that's a one-line route change after the split — the split is the real work.
- **`/memory` becomes entities-only** — which is already its default view, so existing links keep working and the migration is nearly free. Entity details stay under it (`/memory/people/jane`). One practical reason to keep *some* prefix rather than promoting entities to `/$owner/<type>` directly: entity type slugs are user-defined and would collide with reserved routes (`agents`, `connectors`, `settings`…). The prefix is namespacing, not ceremony.

On naming — I'd retire "Context" as a nav label, but I wouldn't jump to "Graph" either:

- **"Context"** is great positioning vocabulary (it's literally the company's context-layer story) but vague as a place name — it doesn't tell you what you'll see when you click.
- **"Graph"** is honest about the structure (entities + relationships genuinely are one) and reads well for your dev audience, but it *promises a visualization* — users clicking "Graph" expect nodes and edges, and today they'd get a list browser. Save the word for the day you ship a relationship-viz view; it'd be a great name for that view *inside* memory.
- My pick: **"Activity" and "Memory."** What happened, and what we know. "Memory" is already the brand the agents speak (`save_memory`, `search_memory`), the URL already matches, and the pairing needs no explanation.

So: sidebar reads Activity / Memory, routes are `/activity` and `/memory`, home stays curated with an escalation link, "Graph" goes in the back pocket for a future viz. This also composes cleanly with the external-agents plan — those deep-links point at `/activity?client=…`.

Want me to build the split? It's one owletto PR: un-redirect `/activity`, move the events pane there, redirect `/memory?view=events` the other way, relabel the sidebar.

# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), use the `agent-browser` CLI with a session cookie minted from the DB. The user's regular Chrome doesn't expose a remote-debug port, so `--auto-connect` will land on the wrong tab — mint a cookie instead.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs
agent-browser --session lobu-verify click @e13        # interact
agent-browser --session lobu-verify screenshot --full /tmp/out.png
agent-browser --session lobu-verify close
```

## Driving the paired Owletto extension (connector debugging)

The cookie-forging above and `claude-in-chrome` both drive a *separate* browser that lacks the user's real logged-in sessions — Revolut, for instance, redirects them to `sso.revolut.com/signin`. To run JS or browser actions in the **paired Owletto extension** (the Chrome that holds the user's live sessions, which is what extension-scrape connectors like Revolut/LinkedIn use), go through the connector-operations bridge instead. No deploy required.

`lobu connector run` is the wrong tool here — it only does local Playwright/CDP against a `browser_session` auth profile, so it errors `Missing --auth-profile` for device-worker connectors (Revolut has no auth profile).

---
name: feedback-concurrent-agent-worktree-wipe
description: Concurrent automation deletes/guts worktrees + submodule checkouts; commit+push the submodule BEFORE any long verification
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

On 2026-07-28 a concurrent agent/automation on this machine twice destroyed in-flight work in `.claude/worktrees/`: first it deleted the whole `activity-memory-split` worktree (uncommitted owletto changes lost, reconstructed from conversation context), later it gutted the recreated worktree down to `packages/owletto` and de-registered it (`git worktree list` no longer showed it; git commands inside fell through to the MAIN checkout — which it left sitting on a feature branch). Disk was also at 99% with the automation re-installing node_modules in worktrees as fast as caches were cleared.

**Why:** worktrees are shared mutable state between sessions; a cleanup/bump job prunes what looks stale, and uncommitted submodule changes don't make the outer worktree look dirty.

**How to apply:**
- In a submodule worktree, `git commit` + `git push -u origin <branch>` as soon as a coherent chunk exists — BEFORE running long gates. Pushed commits survived both wipes; working trees did not.
- If a worktree's git commands start reporting main-repo branches/paths, STOP — the worktree is orphaned and every git command is hitting `~/Code/lobu`.
- Recovery trick: a plain `git clone --reference-if-able ~/Code/lobu/.git/modules/packages/owletto` dropped into `packages/owletto` works fine in place of the submodule; and symlinking the worktree-root `node_modules` to the main checkout's resolves the workspace deps without a 2GB install.
- Disk full on this box: safe reclaims are worktree `node_modules`/`dist`, `~/.bun/install/cache`, `~/Library/Caches/{bun,ms-playwright,org.swift.swiftpm}`.
